Can the Tour Be Pogačar-Proofed? The 2027 Tour de France Route Is Designed to Keep the Racing Close.

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1554 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it’s early November, which means the Halloween candy is on sale, the piles of leaves in my yard are getting harder to ignore, and the routes for the 2027 men’s and women’s Tour de France have finally been unveiled.
  • According to recent reports, first, let’s address the Slovenian elephant in the room: There’s little anyone can do to defeat a healthy, in-form Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates XRG), who will head into the 2027 Tour as the overwhelming favorite to take a record-breaking sixth overall victory.
  • Rather than create a race designed to defeat him, which presently doesn’t seem possible, they’ve laid out a course that could at least prevent the five-time champion from running away with it in the first week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it’s early November, which means the Halloween candy is on sale, the piles of leaves in my yard are getting harder to ignore, and the routes for the 2027 men’s and women’s Tour de France have finally been unveiled. After weeks of refreshing Tour rumor sites, here’s what stood out to me about the men’s route.

According to recent reports, first, let’s address the Slovenian elephant in the room: There’s little anyone can do to defeat a healthy, in-form Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates XRG), who will head into the 2027 Tour as the overwhelming favorite to take a record-breaking sixth overall victory. Certainly, the organizers seem to feel the same way.

Rather than create a race designed to defeat him, which presently doesn’t seem possible, they’ve laid out a course that could at least prevent the five-time champion from running away with it in the first week. The 2027 Tour packs more than 53,000 meters of elevation gain and 28 second-, first-, or hors catégorie climbs into its 21 stages. But there are only three summit finishes, and the first doesn’t arrive until the end of Stage 9, atop the Grand Colombier.

That means fewer chances for Pogačar and his team to jump out to a huge early lead on the Tour’s general classification and then ride defensively, slowly wearing down the opposition until the final week. That’s when the Slovenian usually delivers the coup de grâce, adding a few more stage wins to his ever-growing tally.

Recent findings suggest that yes, there are a couple of punchy uphill finishes in the opening week, at the end of Stages 4 and 5, and Pogačar will do well on them. But the time gaps shouldn’t be huge, so I expect a tighter bunch of riders at the top of the GC heading into the first individual time trial on Stage 7.

Speaking of time trials, the 2027 Tour features 71 kilometers of them across Stages 7 and 16, the most we’ve seen since 2012. It’s hard not to see that as a nod to Belgium’s Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull–Bora–Hansgrohe), the four-time world time trial champion who finished second in the Tour this past July.

Sources indicate that if he can improve his preparation for this year’s Tour, and he’s only 26, Evenepoel could use those time trials to his advantage. The first might even give him a chance to give Pogačar a scare before the mountains arrive at the end of the opening week.

But waiting until Stage 9 for the first mountain stage doesn’t mean the opening week will be easy. A slew of long, tricky stages will be tough for one or two teams to control. And at least until the Stage 7 time trial, plenty of riders should be in contention to spend a day or two in yellow and willing to take a few risks and big swings to make it happen. That’s the downside of designing a route that attempts to delay the GC fireworks until the second week. More riders feel they have a chance to wear yellow, which can lead to more risk-taking and, unfortunately, the possibility of more crashes.

Throw in tight roads, punchy climbs and descents, some rain during the three opening stages in the United Kingdom, and perhaps a few days of crosswinds, and you’ve got the exact right mix to create unpredictable and downright chaotic racing.

If Pogačar is going to run away with another Tour, I expect we’ll know by the end of Stage 11, the final day in the Alps and the second of the race’s three summit finishes. If his rivals, including Evenepoel, Denmark’s Jonas Vingegaard (Visma–Lease a Bike), and France’s Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM Team), can somehow limit the damage on Stages 9, 10, and 11, we could have a much more compelling Tour than what we’re used to.

A run of sprint and transitional stages follows before the final week, when the second time trial and two days in the Pyrenees await. With any luck, we’ll still have a GC battle worth watching by then.

That’s what the organizers appear to be hoping for with this route. But given what we’ve seen from Pogačar and his UAE squad in recent Tours, I’m not sure it will happen. While the time trial kilometers seem to acknowledge Evenepoel as one of Pogačar’s greatest threats, I also see the route as a not-so-subtle gesture to Seixas, the young Frenchman many consider the rider most likely to be Pogačar's successor.

Industry observers note that seixas, now 20, raced his first Tour this past summer and finished fourth overall. The 2027 course should give him a chance to continue growing as a Tour contender without throwing him in at the deep end the way this year’s route did. The French would be thrilled to see him finish on the final podium, and with the Tour’s most intense stages broken into two- or three-day chunks, with time to recover and regroup in between, that kind of result looks well within his reach.

Sources indicate that I’m also eager to see how two-time Tour champion Vingegaard tackles the race. Recent routes have forced Vingegaard and his Visma–Lease a Bike team to burn a lot of matches early, leaving them powerless when Pogačar and his UAE teammates throw down in the second and third weeks. The 2027 course should allow Vingegaard to ride a bit more under the radar, hopefully keeping him fresh for the Stage 7 time trial and the first summit finish on Stage 9. If all goes to plan, the Dane could enter the third week ready to challenge Pogačar in a way we haven’t seen since Vingegaard won his second Tour in 2023.

As for specific stages, I’ve already marked a few as days I won’t want to miss.

In a recent development, the Tour begins in the United Kingdom with three stages that should generate some intense battles among sprinters and Classics riders. Of the three, Stage 3 looks like the hardest. Its 223 km route includes a slew of punchy climbs, making it a perfect day for riders like Mathieu van der Poel (Alpecin–Premier Tech), Wout van Aert (Visma–Lease a Bike), and Tom Pidcock (Pinarello–Q36.5 Pro Cycling Team).

According to recent reports, then there’s Stage 10, a 171 km ride from Annecy to Sallanches that features six categorized climbs and previews the course used in August’s world championship road race. Coming right after the Tour’s second rest day and sandwiched between summit finishes on Stages 9 and 11, this should be an exciting and hard-to-predict day for the GC contenders.

Stage 14 takes the riders 199 km from Montpellier into the Cévennes, covering many of the roads immortalized in Tim Krabbé’s The Rider, one of the best cycling novels ever written. Seriously, if you’ve never read it, find a copy and enjoy! The stage ends on an airstrip just past the summit of the Côte de la Croix Neuve, a famous climb that always generates an exciting finish.

Recent findings suggest that after taking a back seat in recent Tours, the Pyrenees close out the mountain racing in 2027, highlighted by Stage 18. The Tour’s “queen stage” runs 174 km from Pau to Saint-Lary-Soulan, with 5,400 meters of elevation gain and perhaps the two toughest climbs in the entire race: the Col du Tourmalet and a summit finish on the Col du Portet. If the race hasn’t been decided heading into Stage 18, it should be by the end, even with one relatively milder day in the Pyrenees still to come.

And what about Stage 21? Maybe you heard the pre-announcement rumors that the organizers would skip the cobbled Côte de la Butte Montmartre. Thank goodness they proved false. Adding a few trips over the climb to the final stage in 2025 has proven to be one of the greatest innovations in Tour history, and I’m thrilled they kept it in for another year.

Overall, the 2027 men’s Tour stacks up like this: 3,479 kilometers (2,162 miles) spread over 21 stages, with seven flat stages, six hilly stages, six mountain stages, two individual time trials, and three rest days.

According to recent reports, with about eight months to go before the riders hit the road in Edinburgh, a lot can still happen. Most of the top contenders haven’t even confirmed their 2027 programs, which means there’s a chance, however unlikely, that at least one of them might not participate.

Industry observers note that but as long as Pogačar is racing, the result, for better or worse, might be a foregone conclusion. And that’s not necessarily a bad thing. He is a once-in-a-lifetime talent, resetting the record books of the sport the way Eddy Merckx once did.

According to recent reports, but as the saying goes: it’s the journey—not the destination—that matters here. Yes, we should enjoy speculating about who will and who won’t win the Tour de France—and how and when they manage to do it. But we can’t forget that the Tour de France offers at least 21 chances for something exciting and unexpected to unfold. Next year’s route might not prevent the inevitable, but it will certainly produce lots of great racing along the way. And I can’t wait.

How Fast Do You Actually Lose Strength? Slower Than You Think

📅 10 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (748 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdfitness

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You lose strength much more slowly than you probably think.
  • A few days off changes basically nothing, measurable losses take roughly two to four weeks depending on the quality (muscle endurance fades first, maximal strength last).
  • Muscle memory makes rebuilding faster than building the first time, and maintaining takes a fraction of the training that building did.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You lose strength much more slowly than you probably think.

A few days off changes basically nothing, measurable losses take roughly two to four weeks depending on the quality (muscle endurance fades first, maximal strength last).

Muscle memory makes rebuilding faster than building the first time, and maintaining takes a fraction of the training that building did.

Here’s the timeline, and how it can inform your training.

Has this question ever crossed your mind:.

It has been revealed that this was an awesome question that Charles sent my way. (Thanks Charles! 🙌).

When life gets crazy and you find yourself skipping workouts, there’s a voice that indicates:.

I had that exact thought the first time I had to take significant time away for a back injury.

And heck, just recently my kiddos brought home the “crud” from school and I missed a full week of workouts.

So, let’s look at what actually happens, and what it means for your training.

Short version: a few days off doesn’t impact your maximum strength or muscle size basically at all.

Your muscles may look or feel “flatter”, but that’s because stored water and glycogen decrease, not because you are weaker.

According to recent reports, and this “pump” comes back rapidly once you start training again. 💪.

Here’s a rough timeline of when we start to see the effects of detraining:.

Highly trained folks and older adults will notice detraining faster than new or younger lifters (so they’ll sit towards the beginning of these timelines.).

But you don’t lose your progress in any meaningful way after a week or 2 away from the gym. 😊.

And if you DO have to spend significant time away for whatever reason, I have good news for you, too:.

“Muscle memory” is a real thing.

1) Your nervous system remembers how to do the movement.

The first session or two in the gym after time away may feel a bit clunky, but you’ll rapidly regain the technique.

And a significant component of strength is neuromuscular coordination (i.e. your brain and muscles firing together more efficiently, which improves rapidly.).

2) The muscle itself seems to hold onto some of the machinery it built, so it rebuilds faster the second time.

A general rule of thumb is about 50% as long as you were away (so if you were away for 12 weeks, it may take ~6 weeks to rebuild your strength.) Take this with a grain of salt as there is a LOT of variation here. This isn’t a hard and fast rule.

(And you don’t want to jump right back in at 100%. Use the 50/50 rule to get yourself going again.).

The point is, it’s generally easier to rebuild than to build the first time.

The work you did before still counts.

Building muscle and strength? It takes time and effort.

No one wakes up a day after a workout and has just magically put on 5 pounds of muscle.

But maintaining what you’ve built?

That takes only a fraction of the volume.

According to recent reports, when you keep intensity the same (i.e. how hard the exercise is), doing 1/3 the number of sets maintains your strength for a loooong time. ​ The point being: doing ANYTHING during a period where you aren’t able to consistently work out is still really really helpful!

When life throws you off track with your fitness goals, you’re not starting back from square zero.

And even a single session each week with a couple challenging sets is enough to hold what you’ve built until things calm down.

Recent findings suggest that there’s that old saying that: “The best time to invest was 20 years ago. The next best time to invest is today.”.

I think the same holds true for building up your fitness.

Every session you put in now is strength you get to keep later.

According to recent reports, this is exactly why we built our coaching program. Because having a coach makes both of those so much smoother. ​ We take the thinking off your plate so it’s easier to get going.

We direct your limited time and effort toward the stuff that actually moves the needle. ​ AND when life pulls you away (sick kids, a work deadline, etc.) we help you maintain and get right back at it. ​ If that sounds like the kind of help you’ve been looking for, here’s how NF Coaching works. 💪 ​ -Matt.

My friend Sean Mullaney, the FI Tax Guy, recently published an interesting article about the potential downsides of annuities. One of his observations is so simple that I think it's easy to overlook:.

Industry observers note that most Americans already have an annuity. It's called Social Security.

Recent findings suggest that think about what an annuity is trying to accomplish. You give up some control over a pool of money in exchange for a predictable stream of income, often for the rest of your life. Social Security already provides lifetime income, with the added benefit of inflation adjustments.

For a married couple receiving substantial Social Security benefits, that could represent tens of thousands of dollars of annual income that they don't have to generate by selling investments.

Why You Keep Falling Off Your Fitness Routine (and the 2-Minute Initiative That Fixes It)

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Expecting yourself to stick to the same fitness routine, no matter what, is why it fails.
  • Because the only predictable thing about life is that it’s unpredictable.
  • You can’t know which one is coming or when, but you can know something is, and you can build your routine to expect it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Expecting yourself to stick to the same fitness routine, no matter what, is why it fails.

Because the only predictable thing about life is that it’s unpredictable.

A kid gets sick. Sleep falls apart. The to-do list explodes.

You can’t know which one is coming or when, but you can know something is, and you can build your routine to expect it.

That’s the whole trick: take two minutes and decide, in advance, exactly what you’ll do the next time life goes sideways.

Here’s the coaching conversation that reveals how it works.

I want to let you in on one of my biggest lessons from the last 15 years of coaching.

Industry observers note that once you know it, it will feel like you can see the future. 👀.

On a live Q&A, George (not his real name) told me about a pattern he kept running into.

Recent findings suggest that he’d start strong. A few good weeks.

Then a kiddo would get sick, or some other responsibility would pop up, sleep would fall apart for a bit, and the whole routine would go with it.

And he got this look like “Oooooohhhhhhhh…no. No I haven’t.”.

He’d been treating the sick kid as something that happens to the plan.

Not as a predictable part of the plan.

So we talked through it right there. Here’s what we came up with:.

Now, he wasn’t just reacting in the moment, trying to “gut it out.”.

He knew exactly what to do and it fit what he needed.

Here’s the thing: these moments don’t come out of the blue. They are predictable.

Your sleep is going to get messed up.

You’ll have WAY too much on your to-do list.

You’ll forget your gym bag at home.

Your motivation will come and go.

I don’t know which one, or when exactly, but I do know that it’s inevitable.

Once we accept that the only predictable thing is that life is unpredictable, we can use that to our advantage.

Take two minutes right now and finish this sentence:.

First blank: the thing that knocked you off track the last time you were trying to get into a fitness routine.

Second blank: the best version of your plan you can still commit to on one of THOSE days.

Sometimes, life will throw something at you that you REALLY didn’t see coming.

But the more of these you’ve been through, the clearer the crystal ball becomes.

And the better you get at navigating it. 💪.

It has been revealed that hit reply and send me your crystal ball plan. I read every one, and I’ll tell you if I’d tweak it.

Our 30 Unwritten Rules of Triathlon

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1074 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tim Heming outlines the comical 30 unwritten rules of triathlon that every athlete should know.
  • According to recent reports, like a lot of sports, triathlon is full of rules.
  • However, and particularly helpful for beginners, there are plenty more unwritten rules that we need to be aware of.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tim Heming outlines the comical 30 unwritten rules of triathlon that every athlete should know. (Photo: Challenge Family).

According to recent reports, like a lot of sports, triathlon is full of rules. For example, you’re not allowed to cut the course, have a motor on your bike, curse at officials, punch a rival, or, most craven of all, have fewer than three safety pins on your race number in France.

However, and particularly helpful for beginners, there are plenty more unwritten rules that we need to be aware of. Some of them, we’ve helpfully outlined below:.

Sources indicate that 2. Forever Alone — The training paradox. The more you do triathlons, the more all your friends are triathletes, and the more you will train alone.

Sources indicate that 3. You Are Not Kristian — The Norwegian Method is to train more hours in a day than you do not train. For more training methods, see YouTube.

Recent findings suggest that 4. The Devil’s in the Details — Dedicate 20 hours a week to training for three months in the lead up to your A race. Spend zero minutes working on transition.

It has been revealed that 5. Shelve Twitter Hate — Write a mantra on your water bottle and start an Instagram account for reels, stories, and collabs. Don’t be an angry person on Twitter. That’s not cool.

Industry observers note that 6. Match at All Costs — Never sacrifice style for performance. Color-coded kit and equipment are essential, unless you’re going for garish retro, which is an acceptable look for 2026 only.

According to recent reports, 7. Weather or Not? — Check the weather forecast and water temperature before checking the weather forecast and water temperature, and then solicit opinions on what the weather and water temperature are likely to be on race day.

8. Wetsuit Your Worries Away — Convince yourself you can’t swim without a wetsuit/won’t be able to get your wetsuit off if it’s a wetsuit swim.

In a recent development, 9. Experience Equals Complacency — The athlete guide must be studied with a focus that inversely correlates to how many races the athlete has done.

Recent findings suggest that 10. Selfie First, Reality Later — Take a selfie with the giant M-Dot “Ironman Is In Town” sign. Post this to social media as soon as you land, feigning a smile because although you’ve arrived, your bike hasn’t yet followed.

11. Hell’s Bells — Set three alarms minimum and then wonder why the first of them is going off as you force-feed yourself rice because you couldn’t sleep anyway.

According to recent reports, 12. Nothing Matters as Much as Everything — Take time to stare at your race tattoo, realize the transfer has only half stuck, and have a mild panic by convincing yourself you’ll be disqualified before the start.

13. Apply Liberally — Use sunscreen, making sure you miss a key patch of skin. It will show more of your suffering.

According to recent reports, 14. Pay it Forward — In the name of karma, offer to: a) Zip up someone’s wetsuit; b) Lend them a bike pump (even if it’s not yours); c) Thank everyone you see profusely and wish them all a great day.

According to recent reports, 15. Ride the Intake Earthquake — Increase your volume of carbohydrates per hour exponentially with the same dedication you had when you raced 15 years ago and were insistent on using only your 5% body fat as a fuel source.

16. Be a Bathroom Banterer — Talk with bravado about your trained ability to both pee in the swim and on the bike while you stand for an hour in a revolving porta potty line.

In a recent development, 17. What’s Good for the Goose is Good for the Gander — Oops! You punched someone in the eye in the swim completely by accident. Also, the breaststroker you got stuck behind at the first buoy deliberately kicked you in the face.

It has been revealed that 18. Meditate on Aquatic Paradoxes — During the swim, reflect on: a) Whoever learned to swim as a kid is basically a cheater. Or b) “Why do triathletes swim so freaking slowly?”.

19. Style Reigns — Replace existing drink bottles on the bike with those from the on-course sponsor. Call bottles bidons if you’ve ever watched a clip of the Tour de France.

20. The Refs Need You (Really) — Become militant about drafting and shout obscenities at a pack who: a). Aren’t in the race anyway; b) Are out for a gentle social weekend ride; c) Are still moving faster than you.

Sources indicate that 21. Ride the Highs and Lows — When you are riding downhill, you think you will win. When you are riding uphill, you think you will come last.

22. Roll the Dice — Breathe a sigh of relief when you complete the bike leg without puncturing because you haven’t practiced changing tires for five years.

In a recent development, 23. Don’t be Patronizing Pat — If you pass someone on the run, resist the urge to tap them encouragingly on the back. One athlete’s chirpy come-on is another athlete’s patronizing pat. And if you must do it, always avoid the backside.

Recent findings suggest that 24. Leave Self-Awareness Back at the Hotel — Do something in the finish chute that in any other walk of life you would find cringey. This includes sweaty mess marriage proposals to a long-suffering partner who has a cooked neck from staring at a race tracker for the past 14 hours.

25. Be Congratulating Carl — Always congratulate the first person you see at the finish. However hollow-eyed your expression or soiled your tri suit. It’s your duty to have that mutual moment with a complete stranger.

26. The Rules of Race Photography are Unbending — Acknowledge that official race photographs only ever capture: 1. Grotesque faces. 2: When you “briefly” sat up out of aero. 3. Ugly heel strikes.

27. You’re the Best — Use multiple filters of the race results, including but not limited to age-groups, disciplines (including transitions), and nationalities to claim a top-10 position at some aspect of your race. If you rode a road bike, you can also disqualify everyone who rode a TT/tri bike.

28. Brutality Reigns — Include the word “brutal” at least three times during any social media race report.

📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

We Tested 15 Electric Mini-Inflators. These Tiny Pumps Are Fast Enough to Replace CO₂ on Many Rides

📅 13 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2266 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Recent findings suggest that pumping up tires is a constant of cycling.
  • Some riders don’t worry about the exact psi in their tires, but others constantly check and analyze their air pressure, and the latter group may be onto something.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Recent findings suggest that pumping up tires is a constant of cycling. Whether you’re checking pressure before a road ride, fixing a mid-ride flat on your gravel bike, fine-tuning your air pressure at the trailhead, or topping up tires on your kid’s bike in the garage, every cyclist needs to put air in their bike’s tires.

Some riders don’t worry about the exact psi in their tires, but others constantly check and analyze their air pressure, and the latter group may be onto something. In his story, “More Speed and Comfort? The Right Tire Pressure Can Give You Both,” Test Editor Dan Chabanov explains that having the correct pressure in your tires provides more confidence and control on rides.

It has been revealed that small, portable electric inflators have recently taken the cycling world by storm and promptly gained popularity with riders. For several decades, traditional pumps (floor, frame, and mini), CO₂ cartridges, and air compressors have been the go-to methods for filling tires. While mini-inflators don’t fully replace these other inflator types, these small electric units are now finding their way into riders’ toolboxes, gear bags, jersey pockets, and seat bags.

Sources indicate that over the last two seasons, we’ve subjected 15 electric mini-inflators to the same tests. We originally tested 11 inflators in 2025. In November 2026, we tested 4 models (from Cyclami, PDW, State, and Lezyne) and updated our Best Mini-Inflators ranking. A handful stand out for specific use cases or rider types. But these are only a few of the great pumps out there; choose the one that best fits your needs and budget.

With svelte dimensions and a 106-gram weight, the Ultra Tiny is small enough to stash in a jersey pocket, flat kit, or bar bag. Plus, it promptly inflates tires of all sizes to pressure. The AS2’s super-accurate gauge also makes it worth considering for your home shop or carrying in a race-day tool kit. However, the pump runs a little hot.

Industry observers note that at the media launch for the Colnago G-5X, someone asked the brand representatives if any inflators fit inside the internal frame storage. That led me to search for options that can fit inside frames. The Cyclami A5S came up in some discussions, so I ordered one on AliExpress to test.

In a recent development, overall, it’s a solid little inflator that performs well—sub-one-minute inflation times and a 122-gram weight. The rounded profile and placement of the air chuck (on top rather than the side) help it squeeze into many frames’ internal storage doors. Of the five road, gravel, and mountain frames in the office I checked, the A5S fit into four (it didn’t fit into the Cervélo Caledonia).

It has been revealed that several Bicycling editors rely on the Air Rush on rides and at home. Overall, it’s a solid and dependable pick. It has a nice display, runs cool, and inflates road and gravel tires in under a minute. It also filled five road tires; that’s better than most units. I only wish it were slightly smaller for carrying in a seat bag or internal frame storage.

It has been revealed that like many RockBros products, this mini-inflator isn’t the best at any single thing, but it does everything pretty well overall. It gets tires up to pressure in under 50 seconds, doesn’t run too hot, isn’t too loud, and isn’t super heavy.

Recent findings suggest that the most expensive model in our test, the Ultimate, lived up to its name, hype, and steep price tag. And matching its durable appearance, this inflator is a beast—it gets tires up to pressure in under 30 seconds and inflates eight tires on a single charge. I tested Silca’s claim that the Ultimate will seat tubeless tires—surprisingly, it succeeded.

Sources indicate that the Ultimate was the quietest inflator in our testing and tied for the second-lowest temperature. Other than price, the biggest negatives are the Ultimate’s weight and size. One note: after almost a year of frequent use, an O-ring inside the pump failed. However, Silca offered to replace the unit under warranty.

The Pocket SE doesn’t feature a display or gauge, but at only 90 grams, it weighs less than a single CO₂ cartridge and head. And though it takes roughly a minute to inflate a tire to full pressure, I can fill four tires on one charge. The Pocket SE’s one downside is that without a pressure gauge or a 72 psi cutoff, I’d be cautious using it on hookless tubeless road wheels.

For a year, I’ve carried the Pocket SE in my seat bag for flat fixes, and it has gotten me out of plenty of jams. My only complaint is that the button activates easily; a bump or pothole can trigger the unit if it isn’t carefully positioned in your bag.

Portland Design Works makes well-crafted, usable gear for everyday cyclists. The brand doesn’t take itself too seriously, and its products sometimes have whimsical or quirky elements (like its water bottle cages).

Recent findings suggest that PDW’s Essentials inflator follows this mold—it’s well-designed, looks good, and functions well. The Essentials inflates tires quickly, and the gauge is pretty accurate. Its best feature is presets for different bike types (labeled road, gravel, mountain, and city). You can use these to set your tires for your quiver of bikes, or program them for different rides, wheelsets, or riders in your house.

The screw-on chuck is slightly tricky to use and leaks some air if not fastened correctly. While the unit’s body doesn’t run hot, the hose’s base certainly does: heed that yellow warning tag.

Mini-inflators are pint-sized electric air compressors. Larger electric pumps have been around for many years and are commonly used at home, in the garage, or the workshop. Some people carry electric pumps in their vehicles to air up car or truck tires and fill inflatable rafts or SUPs. Cordless air inflators have been a common sight around World Cup mountain bike team paddocks and cyclocross pit zones for several years.

Yet cyclists only started using these inflators within the last three years, when the prices dropped, the form factor shrank, and battery life increased. Riders soon found electric inflators perfect for the garage or the trailhead. Plus, their smaller size makes them much easier to toss in a bike bag or luggage than a floor pump when flying with a bike.

According to recent reports, several cycling equipment brands have released models tailored to bicycle riders’ tastes and preferences. Some companies have even cut enough weight and reduced the proportions to make electric mini-inflators a viable option for carrying in a jersey pocket or flat kit on rides.

The current crop of bike-specific mini-inflators can be broken down into two groups:.

1) Small enough to bring on a ride, and 2) Everything else.

According to recent reports, of course, your definition of “small enough” might vary greatly from another cyclist’s. If you ride with a bar bag or frame pack, an inflator like the Portland Design Works Essentials or Trek Air Rush might be sufficiently tiny. However, if you carry everything in a ride wallet or obsess about weight, even Silca’s 112-gram Elettrico Micro might be too large for you.

For our testing, we focused on mini-inflators sold by cycling-specific brands and ones marketed for bicycle use. This isn’t an exhaustive test of every inflator available; instead, it provides context to help you choose one best for your needs.

In two years of testing, we’ve evaluated fifteen models across a wide price range ($15 to $160). These include mini-inflators from respected cycling brands, options from smaller companies, and those that fly under the radar.

According to recent reports, to test if size matters, I picked some based on their tidy proportions and low weight. I also chose a couple of larger, heavier options to see whether they push air significantly faster or fill more tires than other mini-inflators. I also bought the cheapest mini-inflator available on Amazon ($14.90 on the day I was shopping) to test it against the pack and see if spending more on a pump really matters.

As with other Bicycling head-to-head product tests (like insulated water bottles, flared handlebars, and wide road tires), we evaluated electric mini-inflators based on real-world requirements, not intricate lab tests. Riders can replicate at home without much fancy equipment.

Recent findings suggest that we inflated the tires to air pressures for a 180-pound cyclist riding a road, gravel, and mountain bike in average conditions (as recommended by Wolf Tooth’s app). For road riders, we recorded the time to inflate a 28mm-wide tubeless tire to 65 psi. We also measured the time to reach 30 psi on a 45mm gravel tire. For mountain bike riders (or folks riding fresh-school gravel bikes), we clocked the time to 20 psi on a 29x2.3-inch tire. To evaluate the pumps without built-in gauges, we measured the pressure they reached after 50 seconds.

After timing inflation speeds for each category, I fully recharged all devices. The next morning, I tested how many times each electric mini-inflator could fill a 28mm road tire to 65 psi from fully flat. To prevent overheating, I let each inflator cool down for ten minutes between fills.

In addition to real-world tests, we also measured three common concerns of electric pump buyers: Temperature, noise, and gauge accuracy. For these tests, I borrowed equipment from my colleagues on the Popular Mechanics test team.

Sources indicate that this included a specially designed fixture that measures bike pump gauge accuracy. Gauge accuracy is notable, especially for riders using hookless tubeless road wheels. Since the maximum allowed pressure for these wheel systems under ETRTO standards is 5 bar (72.5 psi), you don’t want to risk a tire blowing off a rim due to a wildly inaccurate pump reading.

It has been revealed that like other users, I have personally experienced noise and heat build-up issues with electric mini-inflators. Early one morning at Sea Otter Classic, my inflator woke the cyclist in the hotel room next door—my sincere apologies to him! Later, on an All Bodies on Bikes group ride, the inflator I borrowed from another cyclist to change a flat melted the plastic valve of my spare TPU tube.

Lesson Learned: Due to excess heat, always use an extension hose when filling plastic-valved tubes with an electric mini-pump.

“Do I plan to carry this on rides?” you ask when purchasing a mini-inflator. If you answered “yes”, look for lighter-weight and smaller-profile models. If you only plan to use the inflator at home, at the trailhead, or at races, don’t focus on size or weight.

According to recent reports, unless you only need to get out of a jam on the side of a road or trail, look for models that fill more than two tires. This allows you to adjust tire pressure and inflate tires on other bikes or spare wheels (and for friends to borrow before a ride—because you know they will need it).

After evaluating these mini-inflators, my key takeaway is that price doesn’t exactly make it the best for your needs. The most expensive pump in our test has brilliant inflation speed, is the quietest, and doesn’t run hot—plus it fills lots of tires. But it’s too heavy and large for most cyclists to carry on rides. However, spending more doesn’t guarantee better performance either, as some pricier models didn’t outshine the low- or mid-priced models. And, as I found out from testing, you probably don’t want to buy the absolute cheapest possible option either (luckily, this model is no longer available).

Skimming listings for different devices, you’ll notice (from similar design details and parts) that a select few vendors manufacture many electric inflator models for every brand. But even if a mini-inflator shares the same outer silicone protector, case, buttons, or display, it doesn’t mean they’re identical. For example, in our testing, the Rockbros model outperformed the extremely similar-looking Muc-Off Air Mach pump.

Unless you specifically need a lightweight, compact mini-inflator for on-the-bike use, spend a little more for a model with a built-in gauge. A display is super handy, and you can pre-set your desired pressure within 1 psi (some even read to tenths).

Pro Tip: If you buy an inflator without a built-in gauge, time how long it takes to reach your optimal ride pressure from fully flat before bringing it out on the road or trail. Then, when you’re airing up a flat fix, you can count off (or use a timer) to get you relatively close to your riding pressure.

It has been revealed that as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Latest England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

Industry observers note that do you ever feel like you’re stuck at the starting line?​ ​ You want to improve your health and fitness. But there’s so. much. going. on.

In a recent development, every time you try to make a initiative, you get 1,000 opinions on the “perfect” workout. The “perfect” diet. The “perfect” routine.

You’re not sure where to start or what to do.

Recent findings suggest that I hear this story so often that I gave it a name. And a face. 😅.

Sources indicate that (h/t to Leo, our awesome illustrator who makes these images for us from scratch! 🙌 ) ​ Meet Major Overload.

He’s every fitness voice on the internet at once.

Sources indicate that do this. Never do that. Fasted cardio. Never fasted cardio. Carbs are fine. Carbs are the enemy.

The Major loves it when you have 100 tabs open on your browser, but haven’t done a workout yet.

In a recent development, he wants to keep you plugged in to The Matrix. He feeds off of you staying stuck in planning mode while he drains your batteries.

My client Eric ran into him a few months ago.

He’d spent weeks searching for “best at-home workouts to lose fat”. ​ In his words:.

It’s the way I felt when I tasked myself with running Nerd Fitness’s Instagram.

It has been revealed that A million different opinions on how to do it. Hours spent researching. And weeks later, I still hadn’t filmed an actual video yet. 😅.

I was firmly stuck in analysis paralysis.

Same boss battle as Eric. Different rabbit hole.

What got me unstuck was the same thing that helped Eric.

It wasn’t finding the “perfect” strategy or proposal.

1) Follow one strategy and block out everything else for now.​ ​ ​2) Commit to taking some small action, most days of the week.

The first one turned Major Overload’s volume down.

I didn’t need every voice. I needed a simple starting point. One that didn’t have a gajillion hoops to jump through.

The second one is where the learning actually happened.

Recent findings suggest that I didn’t have to be perfect. I had to commit to imperfect reps.

I’ve learned more from a couple of weeks of posting than from all the agonizing I did beforehand.

Here’s what I told Eric, and what I’d tell you, too:.

Recent findings suggest that unless you’re Doctor Strange, scrubbing through 14 million possible futures to find the one where everything works out, you can’t know what perfect looks like. Neither can I. Nor anyone on the internet, no matter how loud they get.

Luckily, you don’t need a perfect blueprint.

Enough structure to get out there and do the thing. Not so convoluted that you never get started.

That’s why we built the Beginner Bodyweight Workout and our Strength Training Templates.

So you stop getting stuck at the starting line, and start putting in the reps.

Moving from planning to action does two things at once.

It breaks the inertia, and it teaches you what fits in YOUR life.

And that’s where the real magic happens.

It’s where you learn that, actually, training later in the evening works better for you than trying to force yourself up at 5AM.

It’s how you discover that splitting your workout up into two 15-minute chunks works better for your schedule.

Or that you prefer training with weights to training with bands.

You won’t know those things until you get out there and try.

It’s just as important to learn what DOESN’T work for you as what does.

Three weeks of taking imperfect action will tell you more about what works for you than three months of listening to Major Overload ever could.

Instead of searching for the “perfect” proposal, build your action plan.

1 or 2 actions you can take this week, small enough to test and see how they feel.

In a recent development, that’s exactly what we did with Eric. ​ We mapped out his first few action steps. Things that fit his life, and he felt confident doing.

It has been revealed that and now? He’s 4-months in and training consistently. Not perfectly. Consistently.

And that’s made all the difference for him. 💪.

According to recent reports, one more thing about Eric’s story I want to leave you with. He also shared this with me as part of our conversation:.

That’s something else I hear all the time. And it’s nothing to be ashamed of!

Sometimes, the bravest thing you can do is to ask for help when you need it.

That’s the whole reason we’re here.

When you’re stuck at step one, overwhelmed by information and not sure what’s worth your time, that’s exactly where a coach can help.

Either way, the goal is to get you out of analysis paralysis and moving forward.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is according to the results of a study of nearly 2,000 people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).1.

In other research, people with IBS said they would take a medicine that carried a one percent risk of sudden death if it would cure their symptoms2—which can include urgent bouts of diarrhea, gas, or persistent constipation.

Sources indicate that some people with IBS experience bouts of abdominal pain they describe as worse than childbirth. These flare-ups can siphon concentration, interrupt sleep, and destroy work productivity.3.

In a recent development, as a result, many people with IBS proposal their lives around the availability of private, clean bathrooms. Fear of a sudden flare-up leads some to avoid restaurants, get-togethers, even exercising in public.

This pervading worry has a name—gastrointestinal-specific anxiety—and it can affect everything from social relationships to overall well-being. It’s also the main reason people with IBS report worse quality of life than people with other chronic conditions, including heart disease, diabetes, and end-stage kidney disease.4.

PN Super Coach Sarah Maughan, certified through Monash University—a global leader in understanding the link between food sensitivities and IBS—has witnessed how lifestyle changes can prevent flare-ups, calm GI anxiety, and allow people with IBS to live the lives they want.

“My hope is for everyone with IBS to know they have options, whether that’s turning to a physician for medication and/or a health coach to learn about lifestyle changes and how to put them into action,” indicates Maughan.

In this article, we’ll hear more from Maughan. You’ll also learn:.

Plus, if you’re a health coach, you’ll learn how to support clients with IBS while safely staying within your scope of practice.

Sometimes referred to as “spastic colon,” IBS is the most commonly diagnosed digestive disorder in the world, affecting about 14 percent percent of adults.5.

It has been revealed that unlike Crohn’s and other inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), IBS doesn’t alter the architecture of the gut. When healthcare professionals use diagnostic imaging, they find no infections, inflammation, damage to the bowel wall, or other evidence of disease.

Years ago, this lack of visible disease led many healthcare professionals to assume that IBS was purely psychological. More recently, however, this thinking has shifted.

Experts now view IBS as a functional neuro-gastrointestinal disorder.

That means the nerves between the GI tract and the brain don’t function optimally, causing the brain to deliver unnecessary pain signals and interfere with typical bowel function.

IBS symptoms can come and go, with some people experiencing months or years of relief only to suffer a severe flare-up that can last hours to weeks.

In addition, not everyone with IBS experiences the same set of symptoms, which can make the condition challenging to diagnose.

The below illustration indicates the range of IBS symptoms.

Researchers are still trying to understand why the gut functions differently in people with IBS. However, they do have a few theories.

In a recent development, according to one hypothesis, the nerve endings in the GI tract may be overly sensitive in people with IBS. This can lead to two different sets of symptoms.

▶ Hypersensitive nerves communicate pain signals to the brain, causing people with IBS to notice digestive processes that other people wouldn’t feel. Tiny gas bubbles may be severely uncomfortable for someone with IBS, for example, but not bother someone without the disorder.

According to recent reports, ▶ Overreactive nerves can trigger GI muscles to contract with too much force, leading to gas, bloating, and diarrhea. If they underreact, the same muscles don’t contract forcefully enough, which slows the passage of food through the intestine and leads to constipation.

Another theory blames disturbances on the gut microbiome, which helps to explain why some people develop IBS symptoms after first having a severe GI illness like the Norovirus.

If you or your client suspect IBS, see a credentialed health professional.

In a recent development, the symptoms of IBS overlap with several other gastrointestinal diseases and health conditions that can require medication, surgery, or medically-supervised lifestyle changes. These include infections, inflammatory bowel diseases, celiac disease, cancer, and food allergies, among others.

It’s especially notable to see a medical professional if you or your client notice any of the following:.

In a recent development, in addition to ruling out other GI conditions, a healthcare professional will also ask detailed questions about you or your client’s symptoms. This information allows them to pinpoint which IBS “type” you or your client might have:.

You or your client’s IBS type will inform what your healthcare professional recommends.

Industry observers note that A healthcare provider might suggest a short course of antibiotics and antidiarrheal medicine for IBS-D. On the other hand, for IBS-C, they might recommend a fiber supplement, non-habit-forming laxative, laxative-like medication, or other medicine that reduces the perception of pain and regulates bowel movements.

In order to get the most out of the visit, you can help your client (or yourself) prepare for a healthcare appointment.

A healthcare professional will likely ask the following questions, so consider the responses beforehand:.

Another way to prepare for your first appointment?

Well, you might not like it, but it’s a good idea to….

Consider keeping a poo diary for a couple of weeks before your appointment.

In the diary, track the frequency of bowel movements and other symptoms. Use the Bristol Stool Chart (below) to take note of the quality of your poo. This information can help your healthcare professional assess whether you have IBS and which type.

(To learn more about the clues your poos can hide, read: 6 reasons you should care about your poop health).

In recent years, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved several new prescription medicines for IBS, along with a medical device that stimulates the cranial nerves behind the ear.

In addition, thousands of research papers have looked at the interaction between IBS and various lifestyle habits, with many promising findings.

Here are five evidence-based ways to reduce the symptoms of IBS (and bonus, many of them are great for enhancing overall health too).

People with IBS who exercise regularly tend to experience fewer symptoms and flare-ups than people who don’t exercise.

When researchers asked people with IBS to walk moderately for an hour three times a week, study participants experienced significant relief from bloating and abdominal pain within 12 weeks.6.

How exercise soothes IBS isn’t fully understood, though.

According to other research, exercise may reduce stress and improve mental health, which, in turn, may help improve communication between the gut and the brain.7 8.

Another theory argues that exercise helps encourage the growth of health-promoting gut bacteria, which may help to break down food more efficiently and decrease inflammation.9.

Anxiety, stress, and depression all activate stress hormones like norepinephrine (noradrenaline) and cortisol, which can:.

Of course, stress doesn’t come with an on/off switch.

Simply telling yourself, “Stop getting so stressed out!” won’t likely help—and may even paradoxically lead to more stress.

That’s why Precision Nutrition-certified coaches like Maughan help clients learn to focus on what’s within their control—such as practicing self-compassion, or experimenting with nervous system regulators like yoga, breathing exercises, and gentle walking.

As the image below illustrates, clients can control how they perceive, respond to, and anticipate stressors—but not always the stressors themselves.

Either way, when clients focus more on what they can control and less on what they can’t, they often feel calmer and more capable.

(If you want to help a client figure out just what’s within their control—and what’s not—try out our free worksheet: Sphere of Control Worksheet).

(Assess your current stress load by taking our free quiz: Do you have a Stress Bod?).

PN coaches have long appreciated and advocated slower, more relaxed eating.

Yes, slow eating helps people fill up on fewer calories—but it also tends to help clients reduce or even eliminate GI woes like acid reflux, bloating, and pain.

According to recent reports, for one, slower eating often translates to more chewing. In addition to mechanically mashing food into a pulp, increased chewing also allows the mouth’s digestive enzymes to pre-digest food. As a result, the stomach and intestines have to work less hard.

Plus, eating in a relaxed setting often lowers stress hormones like norepinephrine and cortisol, making it less likely that they will intensify GI pain signals.

According to Maughan, this can be especially notable for young parents, as it’s not always easy to eat undistracted and peacefully when tending to little ones.

Recent findings suggest that (Sounds simple, but slow eating is more challenging than people think—and a lot more impactful. Learn more: Try the slow-eating 30-day challenge.).

According to research, people with IBS experience more shallow, less restorative, and more interrupted sleep.13.

Because of poor sleep quality, many people with IBS sleep more hours overall than people without IBS—yet feel less rested.

Recent findings suggest that fatigue can then set off a vicious cycle. When people don’t sleep restfully, stress hormone levels tend to be higher, which can exacerbate gut pain.14.

Industry observers note that unrested people also tend to feel hungrier during the day. Cravings for fats and sweets also intensify, driving people to reach for the very foods more likely to trigger IBS symptoms—and wolf them down too swiftly.

Stopping this cycle can be challenging.

As with stress, you can’t simply will yourself to sleep more restfully.

However, the first three strategies—exercise, stress management, and slower eating—can all help.

Some PN clients have found that consuming a smaller dinner earlier in the evening gives their bodies more time to digest before bed. Other clients tell us that a relaxing pre-bedtime routine—a few minutes of foam rolling, a guided meditation, a bath, or some journalling—tends to help.

(Find out the best practices for getting better sleep by checking out our infographic: The power of sleep).

While there’s no one-size-fits-all IBS diet, experts have identified several food categories that are more likely to be problematic for many people. These include:.

▶ Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monosaccharides, and Polyols (FODMAPs), which are a family of carbohydrate-rich foods that are poorly absorbed in the small intestine. Even in people without IBS, these foods tend to slow digestion and attract water. When gut bacteria ferment them, they produce gas, which can stretch the intestinal wall. For most, this slowed digestion and gas isn’t especially noticeable; In people with IBS, it can lead to intense pain. High-FODMAP foods include wheat, rye, barley, onions, garlic, beans, dairy, honey, cashews, some processed meats, and many fruits and vegetables. (More about FODMAPs in the next section.).

▶ Caffeinated beverages and foods, especially coffee, which trigger the release of stress hormones, stimulate the production of stomach acid, increase muscle contractions in the colon, and irritate the lining of the intestine.15.

▶ Alcohol and spicy foods that irritate the gut.16 17.

▶ High fructose corn syrup and sugar alcohols such sorbitol and mannitol, which have been linked to gas, bloating, and diarrhea in susceptible people.18 19.

▶ Fatty, greasy foods, which can slow digestion and attract water, leading to loose stools, bloating, and gas.20 21.

If the idea of giving up all the foods and beverages on the above list has you in a cold sweat, know this….

Not everyone with IBS is sensitive to the same foods and beverages.

In a recent development, “Everyone can have different triggers,” says Maughan. “That’s why it’s so notable to figure out what makes your body feel good and what doesn’t.”.

Some people struggle with apples but are okay with berries. Others can drink green tea but not black. One person might be able to consume five to eight ounces of beer but not 12. A gluten-free diet may work great for some but not others.

In a recent development, similarly, many people find relief by avoiding certain high-FODMAP foods. However, you may only be sensitive to some FODMAPs and not others. If so, eliminating all FODMAPs would be unnecessarily restrictive and difficult to follow consistently.

It has been revealed that for this reason, it can be helpful to try an elimination diet to see which foods and beverages are problematic—along with the quantities you can safely tolerate, claims Maughan. You’ll learn more about elimination diets in the next section.

In a recent development, (Want someone to walk you through exactly how to do an elimination diet? Read: How and why to do an elimination diet.).

In our online coaching communities, we often see people asking some version of the following question:.

Industry observers note that “My client just told me that she has IBS. Am I allowed to continue to coach this person?”.

The answer: Yes, you certainly can.

Industry observers note that as we mentioned, Maughan specializes in helping people with digestive problems. Coaching someone with IBS is no different than coaching a client with any other nutritional goal, she says.

“Because IBS is often largely associated with what someone eats, it’s within a coach’s wheelhouse—with some caveats,” states Maughan. “You can’t diagnose your client with the condition, and you should make it clear that you’re not prescribing a diet for them. In addition, you should encourage clients to seek care from a medical professional, especially if you suspect something other than IBS is going on.”.

To stay within your scope of practice, follow these do’s and don’ts.

Recent findings suggest that elimination diets do what the name suggests: They exclude certain foods for a short period—usually three weeks. Then, you slowly reintroduce specific foods and monitor your symptoms for possible reactions.

Elimination diets work a lot like a science experiment that helps you identify problematic foods.

The phrase “elimination diet” may sound scary and off-putting, as if you’ll be living for months on bland food you have to slurp through a straw.

However, there are many different types of elimination diets, with some much less restrictive than others.

This is an excellent option for people who suspect they already know which foods and beverages trigger symptoms.

It has been revealed that it goes like this: You eliminate up to four foods for several weeks. Then, slowly reintroduce them one at a time to see if your symptoms return.

Let’s say, for example, from experience, you know you feel bad whenever you eat dairy. On the lite elimination diet, you’d eliminate just dairy for three weeks. Then you’d reintroduce it to see how you feel.

If you’re unsure of how food interacts with your GI tract—but aren’t ready for a super restrictive eating strategy, our Precision Nutrition elimination diet is likely the way to go.

Created by PN and approved by several registered dietitians, the proposal removes many of the foods most likely to cause problems, while still including a variety of vegetables, fruits, starches, legumes, nuts, seeds, and meats, so you can continue to eat a well-balanced diet.

Sources indicate that to learn more, download our FREE Ultimate Guide to Elimination Diets. This ebook has everything you need to be successful, including an at-a-glance chart that helps you easily follow the diet, along with recipes, meal ideas, and tip sheets.

Over several years, researchers at Monash University in Australia have developed and extensively studied a low-FODMAP elimination diet for people with IBS.22.

Recent findings suggest that unlike other types of elimination diets, the FODMAP diet is a highly specialized form of medical nutrition therapy. The FODMAP diet’s list of problematic foods (shown below) is anything but intuitive, and the reintroduction phase is more complex than other elimination diets.

As a result, if you’ve been diagnosed with IBS and suspect you have a FODMAP issue, seek the expertise of a FODMAP-certified practitioner. You can also download Monash University’s FODMAP Diet app, which will help you navigate low-FODMAP eating.

In isolation, more knowledge doesn’t always lead to more power.

For example, there’s a difference between knowing that dairy messes with your gut and doing something with that knowledge.

Similarly, you might know that you feel better when you eat a small dinner earlier in the evening, but you may struggle to plan your life so an early dinner happens regularly.

This is where a certified health coach can help.

“Many of my clients already have an idea of the foods that tend to cause them problems,” says Maughan, “But they’re nervous to know for sure because they fear that the knowledge will make eating more challenging.”.

That’s why Maughan assures clients….

Even if you do an elimination diet and you learn your favorite food is contributing to your IBS, you don’t have to do anything with that information.

You can choose to continue to eat your favourite foods if you want, AND you can choose to avoid them when it’s really crucial for you not to experience IBS symptoms, she indicates.

“With knowledge, you have choices,” states Maughan.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gravel has been a growing category for years and looking through the gravel events around the US can feel like you are falling into a doom scroll. When figuring out which one to pick it can be overwhelming because there are so many grinders, group rides, and gravel fondos to choose from.

In a recent development, signing up for an event a few months out can help get you out of a rut by giving you a goal to strive for. Maybe you add strength training over the winter or maybe you do those zone two rides you ignore. Either way finding the right event can reinvigorate your stoke for riding, especially rolling into the winter.

It has been revealed that we gathered a small list of rides from around the country to make it easier for you to set up your gravel calendar for 2027. Whether you want to ride in the mountains of Colorado or the plains of Kansas we have a route for you.

Recent findings suggest that note: Gravel is ever-growing and changing. As such, entry fees and festivities can change year to year. You can generally expect some free schwag like socks, a tee, or a hat with your entry fee, as well as complimentary food, beverages, and event celebrations. Some events are also affiliated with charities and donate a portion of the entry fee to those causes.

Sources indicate that held during late winter deep in the red-dirt country, The Mid South is a tough challenge to prepare for. It could be a sunny, warm, beautifully leg-searing ripping fast day or a freezing, rainy, slick, sticky, gloppy death march for 100 miles. It all depends on what mother nature has in store. As one of the iconic events on the gravel calendar, it attracts a deep field of pros and recreational riders looking to test their fitness and tune-up for the season ahead. Rain or shine, riders are rewarded with a huge, welcoming community in downtown Stillwater, shared camaraderie with more than 3,600 registrants, and finish line hugs from the event’s passionate and animated promotor Bobby Wintle.

This amalgamation of a gravel grinder meets enduro features nearly 60 miles and 8,000 feet of elevation over gravel roads and sometimes sketchy singletrack trails. The organizers crown the winner based on performance on a handful of shorter, timed segments within the ride. So, you can stop and Instagram the massive views of Mt. Shasta and the Eddy Mountain Range and enjoy all the food and beverages at the aid stations. Though this is billed as a gravel race, the course goes through the Gateway Trail network—a popular mountain biking destination in the area—so you’ll find yourself on singletrack with berms and slightly techy rock gardens. This event is for you if you love ripping singletrack on drop-bar bikes.

Note: Grinduro has expanded to other locations around the world, including Wales, the U.K., Italy, Switzerland, Japan, and Australia.

Industry observers note that known as the Super Bowl of gravel, the 200-mile Unbound (formerly DK200) event is undoubtedly the granddaddy of the gravel scene. Its reputation for being brutal is well earned. The Flint Hills are endlessly rolling and covered in sharp, often chunky gravel. It can be extremely windy, stiflingly hot, and covered in sticky peanut butter mud. It is a badge of honor to finish this sinister double century before the 3 a.m. cut-off time.

There’s a lottery to get in due to the popularity of the event and it just opened up. Throw your name in that hat now with drawings to be announced on November 21. With the entire town joining in the celebration of gravel, it’s something to behold.

You’ll find a star-studded deep pro field leading the charge of this challenging high-altitude course, as one of the hallmarks of the race is generous and equal payouts for men and women. The 108-mile main event Black course features 8,189 feet of climbing. The sweeping vistas of the surrounding mountain ranges, lakes, and ranches take the sting out of the long, exposed climbs. The terrain ranges from fast hard pack to soft, sketchy moon dust, and it includes one long, chunky road right at the end. Steamboat is located at 6,900 feet of altitude, and the course tops out at about 8,200, which riders from sea level will undoubtedly feel.

This event in the northern area of Pennsylvania doesn’t have the alpine views of Steamboat or the prestige of Unbound. What it does have is exactly what the name implies—seemingly endless climbing. This year I completed the 115 mile route and I was impressed that we were on very small bits of paved road throughout the over one hundred mile course. When I talked to the organizer, David Landis, after the race he said the area has even more gravel than he can include into any of these loops.

A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

  • Here’s what that looks like inside real coaching conversations.
  • When most people picture “accountability,” they picture a drill sergeant.
  • According to recent reports, someone standing over you going “What were you thinking?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what that looks like inside real coaching conversations.

When most people picture “accountability,” they picture a drill sergeant.

According to recent reports, someone standing over you going “What were you thinking? Why did you skip that? Do you even want this?“.

(And if there’s no drill sergeant handy, we do a pretty good job of beating ourselves up all on our own.).

Here’s the thing: if being hard on yourself worked, it would have worked by now.

Great accountability isn’t built on being a hard-ass.

It’s built on forward momentum and honest feedback.

The drill sergeant questions YOU. Your motivation. How much you want it.

Real accountability helps you try again swiftly.

Then helps you see what you’re doing well and what can improve.

Industry observers note that A client of mine had a hectic week. Travel, out of their routine, workouts missed.

The drill sergeant move is “why didn’t you do your workouts?!” at the exact moment they were already struggling.

“Hey! I know this has been a hectic week. Let’s do some push-ups together. Do a set next chance you get and shoot me a 👍. I’ll do one too.”.

In a recent development, this got a 👍 and a “Thanks for the encouragement! This week has been so hectic my schedule got away from me.”.

That win got them back on the routine.

Then we build off of that by looking ahead to the next few days.

In a recent development, “How’s the rest of this week looking for strength training? I went ahead and put together a few variations in case you’re short on time.”.

When you’re already struggling, the question isn’t “hey, why didn’t you do that?”.

It’s getting the next available win.

Then looking ahead to what’s coming up after that.

But forward momentum is only the first part of the equation.

The second step is giving honest feedback on both the wins AND the challenges.

Sources indicate that to be a neutral observer. To point out what’s going well, what’s not, and suggest how we can improve it moving forward.

Based on the actual human in front of me: their unique goals, motivations, and whatever flavor of chaos they have going on in their own life (work, family, travel, illness, injury, etc.).

According to recent reports, “Hey! I reviewed the strength workout on Friday. Solid work all around here. I can see from your form check video that you’re doing a better job staying balanced across your whole foot on the squat. 💪.

I also noticed that the middle of the week has been tougher to get consistent workouts in. You’ve hit 2 out of the last 4 midweek workouts. I know work has been crazy with the project deadline you have coming up, so my guess is you’re getting buried and it makes it hard to get to the gym. Am I on the right track? I have some ideas for how we tackle that next week that I’ll drop down below in a video for you.”.

Sources indicate that this is the honest part. It didn’t go anywhere!

But instead of berating you for missing a workout, the goal is to look at all the evidence and suggest next steps.

Including if the evidence claims that something MASSIVE needs to change. It’s all on the table.

Accountability isn’t punishment for what you didn’t do.

It’s helping you decide what you do next.

If your week went haywire, before you beat yourself up, take this approach:.
