📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

If a cyclist is able to work strength training into their fitness routine, especially throughout the off-season, then the ceiling for potential power and speed goes up. The challenge is, as cyclists we just want to ride our bikes—driving to a gym, spending an hour or more in the weight room, then driving home is that much less time we’ll get in the saddle.

In a recent development, I’ve spent close to the last decade as a personal trainer, and there is one piece of equipment I have come to prioritize in my home gym—no matter the season. The TRX Suspension Strap System is a versatile, compact, and burlier-than-expected piece of gym equipment. I’ve had the same pair since I was certified almost 10 years ago and they are still in great shape—even after loads of personal use as well as using them for in-home training sessions with clients.

In a recent development, one of the major reasons I continue to use the TRX system in my own workouts is because I can do a full-body strength workout, in a fraction of the time it takes me in the weight room, and I can do it all with one piece of equipment at home. All the TRX system needs is a way to mount it and enough room to do the exercises on the list.

Here, we’ll dig deeper into what TRX Suspension Straps are, why I recommend them to cyclists specifically, and give you a workout to jumpstart your season.

In a recent development, TRX Suspension Straps are a suspension-based training tool designed to be used for bodyweight exercises. They were initially created by Randy Hetrick, a former U.S. Navy SEAL. He wanted to create a piece of fitness equipment that could offer full-body training and fit into a backpack—several iterations later, TRX was born. TRX Suspension Straps are basically a set of adjustable nylon straps that have handles to grab and cradles for feet. Most of the exercises you start with will have both hands on the handles, but as you progress you will start to add exercises with your feet in the cradles instead. The unique thing about this piece of equipment is that it can equally push a high-level athlete as well as offer things like balance improvement exercises. TRX bands can take simple exercises like a plank or a squat and offer modifications to make the exercise easier or create challenging progressions to make the exercise (much) harder. That makes them valuable for cyclists just starting out on a strength-training program or for those of us who have been doing it for years. The other great thing is they pack down really well. I have personally put them in the bottom of a carry-on bag on many trips over the years. You can set them up on everything from a traditional wall anchor to tree limbs and doorjambs. During my in-home personal training days, I had even set them up poolside for a great outdoor session with a client.

Cyclists benefit from some level of strength training off the bike. It’s one of the best ways to build speed, power, and durability. (Our Strength Training for Cyclists program, which is free to members, is packed with training plans, strategies, and expert advice, making it a great place to get started or to elevate your current workouts.) With the TRX system, you can get all the benefits of strength training in with a tool that’s super effective. I like it because you can use it for moves that work your whole body, like an atomic push-up, which is when you perform a pushup with your feet in the bands, or something that isolates a muscle group, like a calf raise. Building a strong and sound core is a key to developing stability through the body.

In a recent development, one great thing about the TRX straps is that almost every exercise you do will help improve core stability. Increasing that stability will allow for better energy transfer through your body as you ride. The straps also are incredible for mobility and stretching, allowing you to get deeper into and out of stretches. They do this by allowing you an extra point of stability when your hands are holding the handles or cradles at the end of the straps.

Industry observers note that if you are setting these up in your home gym, you will need a way to mount the straps. They come with a carabiner attached to the straps, but that has to get clipped to something. I typically use a double-length nylon sling used for climbing because I had a few of these lying around that I retired from my climbing rack. TRX also makes specific straps, wall anchors, and even doorjamb anchors to set the straps up on just about anything you can think of. Pro tip—make sure the anchor you use for the straps is strong enough to hold more than bodyweight.

Recent findings suggest that I have been using my own set of the TRX Straps for over a decade now and they show few signs of wear. During my time as a personal trainer, I used the suspension straps for everyone from elite athletes to people in their seventies and eighties just looking to improve balance and mobility. They can handle everything from explosive training days to core and stability training. For cyclists that are looking to build a stronger core, here are a few of my favorite exercises.

Sources indicate that you can find our complete expert-recommended workout here. The exercises, demonstrated by Susane Pata, TRX senior master instructor, will build the strength, stability, and mobility cyclists need. You can do the warmup moves anytime you want to wake up your muscles before a ride, and the stretches to loosen up when you’re done.

A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

Brooks Running Sale | REI Brooks Running Sale.

Industry observers note that the stability counterpart to the Ghost 18, the Adrenaline GTS is the shoe many of us ran in when we fell in love with running. The 25th iteration is the lightest yet, with a foamy midsole, the brand’s DNA Loft v3, to absorb shock and provide soft landings. The guide rails system is Brooks’s unobtrusive stability tech for neutral runners and overpronators alike. Dense foam on the medial and lateral sides acts as bumpers to help align your knee and ankle.

In a recent development, “This is a fantastic shoe,” mentioned tester Chris Garges, an overpronator and heel striker. “I’ve run in every model Adrenaline dating back to the Adrenaline 3, and this is by far the best shoe in the series. I loved everything from the fit to the ride to the cushioning.”.

Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 Review.

Brooks wanted to change what we should expect when running in a max-cushioned trainer. “We noticed that for some people, they would start running in a neutral shoe and then their body would work extra. So the internal cost was actually increasing,” stated Brooks Footwear PLM and BlueLine Director Nikhil Jain.

Sources indicate that the team set out to create a shoe that would cut that internal cost. The Glycerin Flex has a decoupled heel and Flex Zone; these components allow your foot to flex naturally instead of working against a stiff, beefy platform.

In a recent development, “Testing the Brooks Glycerin Flex was a novel experience for me on multiple fronts,” said Editorial Assistant Michael McDonough. “Not only was this the first Brooks running shoe I’ve ever run in, but it was also the first hyperflexible shoe that I have ever seen—and overall, it was a positive experience. The Glycerin Flex combines the benefits of a daily trainer that allows your feet to work and get stronger with the comfort and protection of a maximalist shoe.”.

Industry observers note that we like the Glycerin Max 2 for run/walking and recovery days. The shoe has 45 mm of DNA Tuned foam in the heel and a 6 mm offset. Its beefiness was off-putting for some, especially for runners hoping to get in some tempo work on their long runs. But testers remarked the cushioning was extremely comfy on slow days.

“I loved how comfortable the sneaker was. I instantly felt supported and it felt like I was walking on a bouncy pillow,” said wear-tester Steph Norman. “This sneaker would be great for easy/long miles where you do not have to worry about your feet hurting.”.

Sources indicate that the popular Brooks Ghost hits the trails. The shoe is outfitted for going off-road with 3 mm lugs on the TrailTack rubber outsole.

Our tester, David Hinkl, appreciated how the shoe protected his feet on gnarly surfaces. “The best part of the shoe for me was the sole,” he stated. “It was beefy enough to prevent sharp rocks and pointy things from getting to my feet. Training is more fun when I don’t have to tiptoe across the trail.”.

The Canopy is iconic. Despite the curtains of rain, monstrous winds, and cold temps, Des Linden was the first American woman to win the 2018 Boston Marathon after 33 years. And she wore the Canopy Jacket. This version of the Canopy (the original is also on sale with 30 percent off) can be packed into a little pouch that’s easy to store in the depths of an overpacked duffel.

Recent findings suggest that the High Point keeps out the rain without overheating. Venting in the back allows airflow, while waterproof fabric and sealed inner seams keep you from getting soaked during a downpour. The jacket also packs down into a pocket.

It has been revealed that these joggers are the softest joggers we’ve tested. They’re great for warmups, cooldowns, and traveling. I should know—I trekked Japan after running the Tokyo Marathon in these.

It has been revealed that the Run Visible not only ensures you’re seen with reflective detail, but it also keeps you warm thanks to Thermolite insulation. Three pockets provide storage. That hi-vis orange color also helps you pop out in low light.

It has been revealed that the Chaser is for runners who love a soft compression short with ample storage. The high-rise Chaser has side pockets for stashing your phone and leg-opening grippers to prevent them from riding up.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Fall riding season is winding down, but Black Friday is right around the corner. Several e-bike companies and retailers have already rolled out great deals and special promotions on some of our favorite and best-tested electric bikes. Now’s the time to score big savings on an e-bike if you’re shopping for a holiday gift or for yourself.

Industry observers note that there isn’t a single type of electric bike or e-bike rider. These zippy, pedal-assist bikes are perfect for enjoying your local bike paths, riding rail trails with your family, or tackling singletrack adventures. E-bikes are also great for your daily commute, basic transportation, and running errands.

With major savings from brands, now is a great time to score a deal to get some rides in before the snow starts falling!

No matter your budget or riding needs—from commuters to mountain bikers, experienced cyclists and brand-latest riders—there is an e-bike for everyone and every age. Our test team rides dozens of electric bikes each year, and these are some of our favorites and the best deals out there right now.

The Aventon Level is our benchmark electric bike. It’s a great e-bike for commuting, running errands, or leisure riding. The Level platform has proven to be reliable, low-maintenance, and fun to ride—and it doesn’t break the bank.

The REC features a 750W hub motor with 80 Nm of torque. The bike also has regenerative braking, upping the range to 75 miles. For commutes and running errands, the Level comes standard with fenders, a rear rack, lights, and suspension.

Riders will also find the Level’s connected features very useful. The Level 4’s ACU (Aventon Control Unit) adds several smart features to the already well-equipped platform. The wheel lock and motion sensor alarm are passive theft deterrents when you stop for a mid-ride coffee or run into the post office. A 4G chip in the ACU enables GPS tracking in Aventon’s mobile app, so you can locate your bike if you forget where you locked it. 4G connectivity also allows you to set geofence restrictions on the bike for teens or housemates.

Compared with earlier Aventure versions, the third-generation model rides smoother and feels more like a premium bike (without the high price tag). Aventon’s newly introduced torque sensor allows more control over the acceleration of Aventure’s 750W rear hub motor. Lighter-weight testers found previous models had too much torque, but Aventure fixed that issue. Additional features include a new head-unit interface, integrated turn signals, a front light, a rear rack, and fenders.

The Aventure 3 is an excellent fat-tire e-bike for commuters—especially on snowy days and gravel paths. Off-road, it excels on doubletrack trails and cinder paths. However, the bike is burly; its weight and components limit its fun on technical singletrack and more aggressive mountain trails.

It has been revealed that aventon also offers a mid-drive version of the Aventure. It keeps the same big, burly character but adds a more premium feel, a smoother, more powerful motor, and an upgraded drivetrain—along with a higher price.

Recent findings suggest that aventon’s Pace 5 REC is a zippy e-bike that’s perfect for weekend cruises around town, the bike path, or even occasional commutes. The brand refined the Pace with a slew of updates, making it one of the best bang-for-your-buck step-throughs on the market. These include connected features (such as GPS tracking and theft deterrence), a powerful 750 Watt motor, regenerative braking, and an impressive 75-mile range. It’s offered in five colors (grey, mint, pink, orange, and teal) and two frame sizes.

The Pace 5 does not come with a rack, fenders, or a suspension fork. If you commute by bike frequently or use your e-bike for running errands, consider paying $200 more for the Level 4.

Buying an e-bike on Amazon can be risky, especially if you don’t know much about bikes or have much mechanical experience. However, sometimes you can find a good deal on a decent bike. At $500, the Heybike Cityscape isn’t the pinnacle of e-bike tech, but it helps you get out and enjoy some rides without busting your budget.

The Cityscape stands out for its combination of low price, practical features (like a rack and fenders), and a UL-certified battery. Unlike some Amazon brands, Heybike offers a U.S. support line for warranty service or product questions.

Includes FREE accessories: Fast Charger, Running Boards, Frame Bag, Cushions, Elite Headlight, Seatpost, Comfort Seat, and Orbitor.

Many riders are attracted to the XPedition’s very appealing price. Discounted to $1,699, the dual-battery model has up to 120 miles of range and a 28 mph top speed. A single-battery version is also available for $1,399; it boasts an impressive 60-mile range. Need even more battery power? The $1,999 Long Range model goes up to 170 miles from a single charge.

These prices make the XPedition one of the most affordable electric cargo bikes on the market. And they’re a solid option for riders seeking an excellent deal on an e-cargo bike. “The XPedition’s capability surprised me”, noted Test Editor Dan Chabanov. “Combined with the Lectric XL panniers and the Essentials package, I comfortably carried several days of groceries for a family of three or one adult passenger.”.

Includes FREE accessories: Rear Rack, Water-Resistant Panniers, Lock, Elite Headlight, Seatpost, Comfort Saddle, Phone Mount, and Mirrors.

If you want power and range in a small package, the XP4 750 is right for you. It’s a fast, zippy Class 3 e-bike (pedal assist up to 28 mph) with a 330-pound payload capacity. To increase the XP4’s function and fun, the 750 has a 1310-watt peak motor output (200 watts more than the standard model) and an 85-mile range.

Whether you’re riding city streets on your commute or out for a weekend ride, this bike is fast, easy to ride, and a blast to pedal.

Includes FREE accessories: Rear Rack, Fenders, Headlight, and Seatpost.

According to recent reports, the XP Lite 2.0 scales back the XP4 750’s top speed and power, with pedal assist topping out at 20 mph, a peak motor output of 819 watts, and a reduced payload capacity of 275 pounds. It also drops the suspension fork found on the XP4, but still delivers an impressive range of up to 80 miles.

However, the XP Lite isn’t simply a stripped-down version of the XP4; it has some major advantages. At 49 pounds (without accessories and options), it’s 26 pounds lighter than the higher-powered model. This makes the Lite much easier to lift and transport. Plus, instead of an 8-speed drivetrain, the XP Lite features a low-maintenance Gates belt drive. That means no greasy chain, no finicky gear adjustments, and a quieter, cleaner ride. Yes, it’s a singlespeed, but the pedal-assist motor easily compensates for all but the steepest hills or heaviest loads.

Includes FREE accessories: Support Seat, Elite Headlight, Suspension Seatpost, and Cargo Package.

Electric trikes are a great choice for many riders, including seniors, people with mobility limitations, and those who need to carry heavy payloads. At $1,699, the Lectric XP Trike2 is an easy-to-ride, stable three-wheeler.

A 750-watt motor with 1,310 peak watts powers the XP Trike up to 17 mph and up to 70 miles of range on a charge. The Trike features a wide, soft seat with back support. Plus, it has a suspension seatpost and suspension fork for added comfort.

Industry observers note that with a top speed of 28 mph, 81 miles of range, a 100mm-travel suspension fork, 27.5”x2.6”, a rack, and fenders, the Adventure Neo Allroad Speed’s name fits it to a T. This bike is built for adventures large and small, from commutes to work in the snow or rain, to gravel trails at your local park.

At $1,200, this Cannondale is 45% off its original price and is equipped with better parts than many lesser-known brands’ bikes priced hundreds more.

Many “step-through” e-bikes lack a truly low-step design, making them difficult for some riders to mount or dismount. However, the CTY e2.1, from REI’s Co-op house brand, has a fully step-through front triangle. This makes the CTY a great choice for older riders, those with mobility limitations, or others who seek an easy-to-ride e-bike.

It has been revealed that REI equips the CTY e2.1 with a 250-watt hub-drive motor; it provides smooth pedal assistance up to 20 mph. It also features a suspension fork to smooth out bumps and potholes, an adjustable stem to custom-tune your riding position, and hydraulic disc brakes for improved stopping power. For less than the cost of many unknown e-bikes online, you can get a quality electric bike backed up by REI’s warranty and service.

According to recent reports, salsa’s Moraine 145 costs less than many hardtail E-MTBs. But don’t let the price fool you; this bike is value-packed. This dual 29-inch-wheeled trail bike comes equipped with Fazua’s Ride 60 motor (60 Newton-meters of torque) and a 430-Watt-hour battery. While it has less torque and a smaller-capacity battery than higher-priced competitors, it has enough power for some serious fun in the woods and on singletrack.

Industry observers note that the frame uses a Split Pivot suspension system designed by Dave Weagle (the mastermind behind the dw-link suspension system on Pivot bikes), for a balance of performance and pedalability. A 10-speed Shimano Cues drivetrain, four-piston Shimano brakes, a dropper post, and Terravail tubeless tires round out the components of this feature-packed full-suspension E-MTB.

Electric bikes are great for commuting and city life. However, their added weight (sometimes as much as 90 or 100 pounds) can make e-bikes a pain to carry up flights of stairs, load onto a bus or train, or even move around in your garage.

It has been revealed that weighing only about 40 pounds, the Roadster v3 cuts weight without sacrificing much performance or adding cost. Ride1Up uses a 500 watt/50Nm rear hub motor with an internal battery for a clean, stealthy look. 700x45c gravel tires carry speed on pavement or hardpack dirt roads, and metal fenders keep the road spray off your clothes.

In a recent development, electric mountain bikes are a ton of fun and help you ride more of your favorite trails. We recommend full-suspension E-MTBs for aggressive and technical trails. But hardtails often work fine on easier trails and mellower terrain, and they cost a lot less than dual-suspension models.

Velotric keeps costs low on the Summit 1 by using a rear hub motor instead of a pricier mid-drive unit. The Summit also features an 8-speed Shimano drivetrain rather than more expensive 11- or 12-speed systems. However, Velotric gives the bike a 120mm thru-axle fork to soak up bumps, Shimano hydraulic disc brakes, and a full-color screen with Bluetooth connectivity.

Electric bikes are a great way for older riders to enjoy cycling and stay active. However, many commuter e-bikes have high top tubes, and even many step-through-style frames still require riders to swing their leg over the frame. The Velotric Discover has a Euro-style, low-step-through frame that makes it easier to get on and off.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that A deep trunk muscle, the QL attaches to the lower spine and the back side of the pelvis, Nicole Haas, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and founder of Boulder Physiolab in Colorado, tells Runner’s World.
  • In a recent development, when you run, the QL plays more of a stabilizing role, working to control your pelvis and trunk while you stride, says Spencer Agnew, PT, DPT, a physical therapist at Sword Health and run coach with Wisconsin-based Ascent Endurance Group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that most runners are familiar with the big muscles involved in running, such as the quads, hamstrings, and glutes. But there are lesser-known—yet still vital—players that can influence running performance. One example: the quadratus lumborum, or QL for short.

Recent findings suggest that A deep trunk muscle, the QL attaches to the lower spine and the back side of the pelvis, Nicole Haas, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and founder of Boulder Physiolab in Colorado, tells Runner’s World. It serves a few different functions in daily life, such as helping you arch your back, bend to the side, and rotate your upper body, Haas explains.

In a recent development, when you run, the QL plays more of a stabilizing role, working to control your pelvis and trunk while you stride, says Spencer Agnew, PT, DPT, a physical therapist at Sword Health and run coach with Wisconsin-based Ascent Endurance Group. The QL also assists with breathing, specifically when you inhale, Agnew adds.

In a recent development, if this muscle is tight or irritated, you’ll likely feel pain in your back or sacroiliac joints, which link the pelvis and lower spine, Agnew indicates. To help you avoid these aches, we asked the PTs to explain what can cause an angry QL and how to relieve it.

In a recent development, there are several reasons your QL might be yelling at you. A common one? Your hip flexors are tight. In particular, when the psoas (a significant, rope-like hip flexor muscle that runs from your lower back to the front of your hip) is shortened, it can pull your pelvis into an anterior tilt, meaning your pelvis is tipped forward, arching your lower back. In many cases, this yanks on your QL as well, because the psoas and QL both insert into the same group of vertebrae in your lower back, Agnew explains.

Sources indicate that another culprit is weak glutes. When your glutes aren’t strong enough to help you maintain good running mechanics, your knee can collapse inward as you land and your opposite-side hip can dip down, Haas explains. This, in turn, can cause your trunk to side bend and rotate, thus placing more strain on your QL over time. Running downhill can exacerbate the problem, Haas adds, because that can cause your lower back to arch and place further stress on your QL.

Yet another cause of an irritated QL is upper-back stiffness. Restrictions in the upper part of the spine can shift more workload onto the QL, Haas explains. So can challenges in your shoulders, hips, and mid-back. If these areas aren’t moving like they should due to pain or injury, your QL may receive added stress, Haas claims.

According to recent reports, keep in mind that in some cases, your QL may hurt because it’s taking on a bunch of extra stress it’s not meant to, but the muscle itself probably isn’t tight. “It’s more like your QL is just irritated because everything has been collapsing around it and loading it,” Haas states. “It’s overworked and underappreciated.”.

A tight-feeling QL is worth addressing because it can lead to a few not-so-great issues if left unchecked. A major one? Compromised running mechanics.

According to recent reports, A tight QL, as mentioned, can shorten your hip flexors and pull your pelvis into an anterior tilt, which will reduce your knee lift as you stride, Agnew notes. As a result, “you’re not going to be able to generate as much force moving forward, and you’ll have more of an arched-back position when you run,” he explains. In many cases, this can deliver a double whammy of reduced performance and increased back pain, he says.

It has been revealed that on top of that, a tight QL can also hinder your breathing. As mentioned above, one of the QL’s jobs is to help you inhale, so when this muscle is tight, you may not be able to breathe as deeply or easily, Agnew notes.

Plagued by what you think may be an irritated QL? Try Agnew’s three-step at-home series to help reduce your discomfort.

Industry observers note that perform this sequence as often as every day if you’re in significant discomfort that’s limiting your ability to run. In the case of minor pain, incorporate this series two to three times per week. On the days you run, perform the myofascial release, pelvic tilts, and hip hikes before you lace up, then tackle the other components afterward.

This can help turn down the pain response in a barking QL by desensitizing soft tissue, Agnew explains.

How to Perform Myofascial Release.

In a recent development, the pelvic tilts help you learn how to coordinate and control pelvic motion so you can maintain proper mechanics while running, and the hip hikes help activate your QL. The kettlebell side bend increases blood flow to the muscle, which can aid in healing. Finally, the suitcase carry increases strength, stability, and engagement of the muscle, which can ensure it functions properly during a run.

Lengthen your QL—as well as tight hip flexors—with this two-for-one half-kneeling lunge stretch.

Do these moves daily or several times per day to mobilize your lower back. Perform them before or after a run. Important caveat: If your QL hurts more after stretching—or if your QL pain returns soon after stretching—then stretches are likely not the solution and you should stop doing them, Haas explains.

Dynamic QL Mobility + Hip 90/90.

To start, do one set of these moves daily to help your body learn the neuromuscular patterns. (The caveat: If you feel sore, then skip a day.) After about six weeks, do these moves two to three times per week as part of your regular strength-training routine.

Recent findings suggest that this exercise targets the glutes and works on pelvic control in a movement pattern that’s similar to running. Think of it as an opportunity to train proper glute use in your running form, which will help unload any strain on your QL caused by weak glutes.

Recent findings suggest that this exercise can improve core stability and strengthen the glutes, resulting in improved running mechanics and less stress on your QL. You’ll need a long, looped resistance band.

Sometimes, despite your best at-home efforts to treat an irritated QL, it’s still best to get checked out by a physical therapist. Haas recommends booking a PT appointment if you try the above stretches and strength moves and don’t see improvements after about two weeks.

Sources indicate that agnew suggests getting evaluated by a PT if you’re in so much pain that it’s inhibiting your running. In this case, getting seen sooner can help mitigate pain before further concerns arise, Agnew explains.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for cyclists, body composition is a critical performance factor that goes beyond aesthetics.
  • Understanding age and typical body fat percentage ranges gives us valuable context for setting realistic and healthy body composition goals and determining whether our focus should be on fat loss, strength building, or overall health.
  • Industry observers note that 🚴🏻‍♀️ Ready to unlock a stronger, healthier you?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for cyclists, body composition is a critical performance factor that goes beyond aesthetics. It directly influences climbing speed, power endurance, and recovery capabilities. Average body-fat percentage averages and recommendations shift as we age depending on individual goals, and whether we’re a recreational rider or a competitive cyclist pursuing maximum power-to-weight ratio.

Understanding age and typical body fat percentage ranges gives us valuable context for setting realistic and healthy body composition goals and determining whether our focus should be on fat loss, strength building, or overall health. (It’s crucial to note that body fat percentage and BMI (body mass index) are not the same thing.).

Industry observers note that 🚴🏻‍♀️ Ready to unlock a stronger, healthier you? Our Cycling for Weight Loss program will help you find confidence and consistency in your training.

Recent findings suggest that there isn’t a universally “right” body-fat percentage. Ideal targets depend on sex, age, activity level, and specific goals, in addition to whether you’re prioritizing general health, recreational fitness, or competitive performance. However, there are commonly used target ranges per decade that coaches, trainers, and sports scientists use as healthy guidelines (which should be treated as approximate).

According to recent reports, let’s examine “average” body fat percentages guidelines by decade, what the average body fat percentages are for men and women in the United States, and the impact of different measurement methods (DEXA scan, home body fat scale, InBody scan) on results. These averages should be regarded as benchmarks for setting achievable, performance-oriented goals, not as rigid targets. They serve as a navigational tool rather than a mandatory destination.

20s: Competitive athletes: 6–10 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 11–15 percent, Healthy range: 12–20 percent.

30s: Competitive athletes: 7–11 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 12–16 percent, Healthy range: 14–22 percent.

40s: Competitive athletes: 8–12 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 13–17 percent, Healthy range: 16–24 percent.

50s: Competitive athletes: 9–13 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 14–18 percent, Healthy range: 18–26 percent.

60+: Competitive athletes: 10–14 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 15–19 percent, Healthy range: 20–28 percent.

20s: Competitive athletes: 14–18 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 19–23 percent, Healthy range: 20–30 percent.

30s: Competitive athletes: 15–19 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 20–24 percent, Healthy range: 22–32 percent.

40s: Competitive athletes: 16–20 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 21–25 percent, 50s: Competitive athletes: 17–21 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 22–26 percent, Healthy range: 26–36 percent.

60+: Competitive athletes: 18–22 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 23–27 percent, Healthy range: 28–38 percent.

Cyclists specializing in climbing typically aim for the lower end of these ranges, though excessively rapid fat loss can compromise strength and power.

While the ranges above are recommended guidelines, the actual averages for folks according to the CDC look pretty different. The following data on average body fat percentage of men and women in the U. S. has been collected through the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.

It’s crucial to note that the body fat percentage measurement method really matters. Home scales that measure body fat percentage can be quite inaccurate according to researchers. In my own experience, an InBody scan (which is the measurement method I recommend for a more reliable assessment, by the way) revealed that my body fat percentage is several percentage points higher than what the home body fat scale I have been testing had measured.

Industry observers note that however, even InBody results can fluctuate with hydration levels. DEXA scans offer the most stable results but are generally more expensive. The key is to track trends over time rather than focusing on single numbers.

Industry observers note that when it comes to fat loss, aim for a safe and healthy pace of 0.5-1 percent of body weight per week, while prioritizing preserving lean mass through optimal protein intake and strength training. However, it can be tricky to determine how much of the body weight lost is fat, and factors like how lean someone already is, a person’s metabolism, and training intensity also play a role.

As an example, in one study of female volunteers on reduced-calorie diets, participants were assigned exercise programs of varying intensity. According to the researchers, the women doing a moderate exercise program lost 6.2 percent body fat over three months on average, which added up to being about 2 percent a month. The intense exercise group lost an average of approximately 10 percent body fat over the same time period, which comes out to around 3.3 percent per month.

Understanding body composition is a valuable tool for cyclists looking to optimize their performance and achieve their goals. By considering your age, sex, activity level, and using reliable measurement methods, you can set realistic targets and tailor your training and nutrition strategies accordingly. Remember, it's all about finding the right balance for your body and your goals.

Sources indicate that natascha Grief is the fitness and reviews editor for Women’s Health. She writes about fitness, health, performance, everyday movement, and the products that help people train and recover better. She brings more than a decade of experience as a NASM-certified personal trainer focused on training women, with specialties in functional strength training, corrective exercise, nutrition, and behavior change. She previously worked as the health and fitness editor at Bicycling, and her writing has appeared in Runner’s World and other outlets. Across her work, she’s especially focused on making complex wellness, training, and performance topics approachable and accessible.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The top spot on the podium was wide open in the women’s race, with the series’ undefeated champion Cassandre Beaugrand (FRA) absent.
  • It has been revealed that 2025 world champion Lisa Tertsch (GER) was the significant name going in, alongside Jeanne Lehair (LUX), who had been part of a sprint finish at the World Cup in Hong Kong the week before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Wagner Araujo/World Triathlon).

Sources indicate that the postponed WTCS Abu Dhabi brought the World Triathlon Championship Series, as it is presently known, to a close ahead of its transition to T50 racing within the Triathlon World Tour. The sprint-distance showdown still attracted many of the sport’s top names, with Olympic qualification points and the chance to finish the season on a high and build momentum into 2027.

The top spot on the podium was wide open in the women’s race, with the series’ undefeated champion Cassandre Beaugrand (FRA) absent. Add to the mix the shorter, sprint-distance format and hot, windy conditions set to play a factor, and it was anyone’s guess who would take it.

It has been revealed that 2025 world champion Lisa Tertsch (GER) was the significant name going in, alongside Jeanne Lehair (LUX), who had been part of a sprint finish at the World Cup in Hong Kong the week before. However, Diana Isakova (RUS) was another athlete many had their eyes on after winning that sprint against Lehair and taking the World Cup win in Rome before that. American Gwen Jorgensen (USA) had shown glimmers of top form in recent races, placing fifth at WTCS Weihai and producing the second-fastest run split at the Grand Final in Pontevedra.

Into the warm, 82-degree water, three groups began to form near the front as the chop and currents made for one of the most difficult swims of the year.

Isakova and Lehair were among the first group out of the water, while Tertsch and Jorgensen exited more than 20 seconds behind. That deficit would swiftly balloon to over 30 seconds early on the bike, with another group between them and the front of the race.

Recent findings suggest that halfway through the bike, the front group of nine maintained its advantage as the third group swallowed the second to form one large chase pack. On such a tight, technical course, the larger group offered little additional benefit as the smaller pack ahead steadily increased its lead.

At the end of the bike, Germany’s Laura Lindemann (GER) almost undid the work of the front, mishandling her bike after the dismount, almost causing a crash. Onto the run, a quick transition shot Isakova to the front, while around 36 seconds behind, Jorgensen and Tertsch were among the large group with significant work to do – and only 5km to do it.

By halfway, Isakova and Lehair were clear at the front, foreshadowing a repeat of the race in Hong Kong the week prior. Jorgensen remained 36 seconds behind but had gapped Tertsch and made her way into eighth place.

Industry observers note that that momentum continued for Jorgensen as suddenly eighth place became third and she could see the leaders up ahead. Unfortunately, the gap was just too large at that point. Isakova made her move with over 200 meters to go, picking up her first WTCS win and cementing her remarkable end to the year.

Lehair finished second and reflected that her efforts on the bike may have affected her run: “I may have used too much energy, but I am super happy with second place and my third podium of the year.”.

Jorgensen couldn’t believe her result, returning to the WTCS podium for the first time since 2016 at 40 years old and producing the fastest run split of the day.

“I thought I was out of this race but one of the coaches told me I was third and I couldn’t believe it,” she shared.

In the men’s race, this year’s Grand Final winner and sprint-distance specialist Matt Hauser (AUS) was wearing bib #1. With his prowess in the water, all eyes were on him in the absence of new world champion Vasco Vilaça (POR). Brazil’s Miguel Hidalgo (BRA), meanwhile, was looking to finally turn his training form into a result after some disappointing recent outings.

In a recent development, newly introduced Zealand’s Hayden Wilde (NZL) was the other big name on the lineup, having recently been approved to race both WTCS Abu Dhabi and Dubai T100. With the races falling within 24 hours of each other, that would not normally be allowed under World Triathlon rules. With his eyes firmly back on the Olympics, this was Wilde’s A-race for the weekend, according to New Zealand’s National Performance Manager Stephen Sheldrake.

According to recent reports, it started with a windy, choppy swim that mostly stayed compact until the return to the beach, when two lines formed toward the shore. One group, including Hauser, made a beeline for the beach to get out of the water as soon as possible and run along the shore toward transition. That worked well for the Australian, who entered T1 with a small gap over compatriot Luke Willian (AUS).

Wilde found himself 39 seconds in arrears, with work to do alongside recent Iquique World Cup winner David Cantero del Campo (ESP). They were in a large chase group aiming to gain time on the lead group of 11, but on such a short, fast, five-lap bike course, their work was cut out for them.

It has been revealed that almost immediately, however, the gap was nearly cut in half, with Wilde driving the chase to within 22 seconds by the end of the first lap. The pace was so hot that the group split apart, with only a few athletes able to go with him on the technical course.

It has been revealed that perhaps that woke up the front group, which managed to limit its losses over the remainder of the bike and reached T2 with around nine seconds on Wilde and company. It was less than they would have hoped for against the stellar Kiwi runner, but the significant question was whether the bike had stung his legs enough to hold him off. A slow transition from the 2025 winner of this race gave him even more work to do.

Onto the run, it didn’t take long for Hauser and Hidalgo to separate themselves at the front. Behind them, Wilde swiftly recovered from his transition losses and moved through the rest of the front group alongside Shachar Sagiv (ISR).

The front two continued to push the pace and began adding time to Wilde behind. Hidalgo made his move before the second lap, and Hauser wasn’t able to respond. He promptly began to lose ground as the Brazilian looked comfortable all the way to the finish, taking the tape with an unmatched 14:20 5km.

It was a much-needed WTCS win to carry momentum into the 2027 Triathlon World Tour. Hauser shared afterward that he “could really feel the legs – and the whole year – in the back end of that race.”.

Wilde crossed the line in third, comfortably ahead of the rest of the field, but a 14:52 5km left him short of the run speed he is accustomed to producing in these races. He won’t have much time to digest the result, however, as he immediately has to travel to Dubai, where he would look to continue his dominant T100 season.

10-Minute Slow Yoga Practice to Counter the Chaos

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that yoga isn’t the answer to everything.
  • Sources indicate that the challenge here, especially when your default state has been “go go go,” is to slow down.
  • Your goal today is relaxation, so you might want to keep a supportive prop—such as like a bolster, pillow, or yoga block—close by.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that yoga isn’t the answer to everything. But when life gets stressful, your mat is a safe place to land. Amid moments of stress and chaos, a gentle yoga flow made up of intentional movement can help still your racing mind, regulate your breathing, and encourage overall well-being. This practice blends elements of yin yoga and a generally pared-down approach that feels like a truly restful beat rather than another item on your to-do list.

Sources indicate that the challenge here, especially when your default state has been “go go go,” is to slow down. It’s almost like you’re retraining your body, and reminding yourself that it’s okay to do so.

Your goal today is relaxation, so you might want to keep a supportive prop—such as like a bolster, pillow, or yoga block—close by.

In a recent development, begin in Rock Pose today, which is a variation of Child’s Pose. Sit back on your heels, with your toes untucked, and keep your legs close together. Hinge forward to round your upper body over your legs, placing your forehead on your mat or a block. Drape your arms by your sides, palms facing upward, so you create a rock-like shape.

Stay here for 1-3 minutes or as long as you’d like.

Extend your arms forward and press up onto your hands and knees. With your next inhalation, lower your belly, lift your chin and chest, and arch your back in Cow Pose.

Exhale as you round your back and tuck your chin in Cat Pose.

Repeat Cat and Cow 3 times each, moving with the pace of your breath.

Recent findings suggest that lower yourself all the way down onto the front side of your body. Widen your feet toward the back corners of your mat. Your elbows will be just underneath your shoulders—or slightly forward if you’re dealing with lower back tension. Then lift your chest and press your palms and forearms into the mat in Sphinx Pose.

If you have a block, you can use it on its highest setting by angling it toward you and allowing your forehead to rest against the support.

Stay here for 1-3 minutes or as long as you’d like.

Still lying down, stack your hands, elbows bent and pointing toward the edges of mat, and rest your forehead on the backs of your hands.

It has been revealed that start to slide your right knee out to the right side of the mat so it’s about in line with your hip in Half Frog. You want your right leg to have about a 90-degree angle so the inner thigh and calf are facing the floor. Keep resting your forehead on your hands or turn your head to one side.

Stay here for 1-3 minutes or as long as you’d like.

When you’re ready, repeat on the opposite side.

According to recent reports, from Half Frog Pose with your left knee bent, take a deep breath in. As you exhale, let your left leg extend long and straight behind you. Drape your arms by your sides, palms facing up. Turn your head and your gaze in either direction and let your shoulders round toward the ground. Simply be.

Stay here in a reverse variation of Savasana for 3-5 minutes or as long as you’d like.

Here’s What to Know About the Nike Vaporfly 5

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (872 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Nike declared a whole slate of innovations it has in the works, including a new method for creating Air units, the return of the Nike Free, and a look at the future of its sportswear.
  • The massive highlight is that the road racing shoe is basically going to have a “spring” in it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Nike declared a whole slate of innovations it has in the works, including a new method for creating Air units, the return of the Nike Free, and a look at the future of its sportswear. But the most interesting product unveiling is the Vaporfly 5—Nike is calling it the “most aggressive Vaporfly yet.”.

The massive highlight is that the road racing shoe is basically going to have a “spring” in it. “At the center of Vaporfly 5 is a upcoming, wave-shaped Flyplate,” Nike’s announcement read. “A ripple through the midfoot creates a spring-like sensation under the arch.”.

I got a look at the prototype in Chicago last month, when I visited Nike’s headquarters during marathon weekend. There, I asked Bret Schoolmeester, vice president of running footwear product, if he was concerned about calling the shoe a spring. He is not, and told me that shoes basically serve as springs already given the bouncy modern foams being used.

Remember back to the first carbon-plated shoes, when much of the uproar around them was because people believed the plates would act like springs. That’s not really what came to fruition, as we found that the plates basically were used as stiffening mechanisms to create leverage.

World Athletics rules permit a plate in a single layer, and that’s what Nike is technically creating here. The difference is in the shaping. The bump in this new plate, combined with the midsole geometry, will allow the plate to flex when you land and snap back to shape to propel you ahead.

Nike also looked at ways to strip weight, which you can see through the major carve-outs in the foam, the super thin Vapor Mesh upper, and sparse use of Goatek outsole. Another weight-saving measure is adding ZoomX LT, the lightweight version of ZoomX that we saw in the Alphafly 4. A thin layer of that sits between the plate and your foot, while the standard ZoomX is used between the plate and the road for control and responsiveness.

Sources indicate that with these changes, Nike is positioning this shoe to be a shorter-distance road racing shoe. Given the overhaul of the Alphafly 4 and the announcement of the Apex, a hyper shoe designed for elite marathoners, the Vaporfly is being pitched for races up to 13.1 miles. Sure, some runners will lace it up for a full marathon, though it’s going to be lighter and snappier to excel at faster speeds.

The shoe won’t be available until “fall 2027,” but Nike is showing it off early as it drums up excitement for upcoming footwear and apparel at its World of Athletes event.

Beyond the Vaporfly 5, there were some other cool new innovations declared, including “Tuned Air.” Through a new manufacturing process, Nike is able to create lighter Air units more swiftly, which can be customized for various applications.

According to recent reports, I spoke with Phil McCartney, executive vice president, chief innovation, design and product officer, last week about Tuned Air. He explained that through a proprietary digital print and selective lamination process, Air units can be created with different amounts of cushioning and support. Those characteristics are delivered not only through the physical geometries of the Air unit, but also by varying the pressure within each unit.

Nike has previously talked about “Tuned Air,” and we saw it in use with the Pegasus Plus 2. But that was really just offering a few different air bags. The idea is that bigger shoes are worn by bigger runners and, thus, bigger Air units with greater gas pressures are required. So, shoes any smaller than a women’s 7.5 (M6) got an Air unit that’s 9.5 mm thick with 15 psi. Moving on up to a men’s 10.5 (W12), the bag gains 2 mm thickness. And, those runners with larger feet sit atop the 11.5mm-thick unit pumped up with 20 psi.

These newly introduced units, however, are different altogether. Nike found a way to remove the need for pins and rigid zones that formed the Air units, so that each can offer better cushioning and responsiveness.

Like the Vaporfly 5, Tuned Air won’t make an appearance until later in 2027. The prototype shoe teased in the image above has one massive Air unit making up the entire midsole. No word yet on which model or franchise that shoe will reside.

While we wait, the fastest Nike available to any of us remains the Alphafly 4.

Recent findings suggest that jeff is Runner-in-Chief for Runner’s World and the director of product testing. He has tested and reviewed running shoes, GPS watches, headphones, apparel, and more for nearly two decades. He regularly tests more than 100 pairs of shoes each year, and once had a 257-day streak running in different models. Jeff can usually be found on the roads, racing anything from the mile to a marathon, but he also enjoys racing up mountains and on snowshoes. When he’s not running, you’ll probably find him hanging from a ladder making repairs and renovations to his house (he’s also director of product testing for Popular Mechanics).

In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Industry observers note that fall riding season is coming to a close, and winter is right around the corner. While late fall and winter mean shorter daylight hours for riding, it’s a great time to save on cycling gear—for yourself or if shopping early for holiday gifts. Many brands are discounting old inventory at great prices, and others are clearing room for new gear hitting shelves after the New Year.

Although many of the best holiday sales aren’t until Black Friday and Cyber Monday, some retailers are running Early Black Friday promotions with substantial deals and discounts on top-rated gear. In addition to Pre-Black Friday sales, Amazon, REI, bike brands, and other retailers are offering deep discounts on cycling equipment, components, apparel, and accessories you need for road, gravel, and mountain bike rides.

In a recent development, pre-Black Friday sales are a great chance to stock up on frequently used consumables—such as tubes, tire sealant, chain lube, and nutrition products—and to grab the gear you need for late-fall and winter rides. They’re also a great way to save money on usually pricey riding apparel: If you’ve been holding out on buying a fresh vest, arm warmers, jerseys, a jacket, or even shoes, some brands are offering deep discounts on cycling clothing and accessories.

Industry observers note that below are sales and deals hubs for several top online cycling gear and bike retailers, plus links to sales from leading clothing brands and bike companies. These are some of the best deals on editor-tested gear we’ve spotted so far. Bookmark this page and return for updates as even more deals come online.

➜ AMAZON ➜ REI ➜ BACKCOUNTRY ➜ COMPETITIVE CYCLIST ➜ BIKE TIRES DIRECT ➜ PEARL IZUMI ➜ VELOCIO ➜ CAPO ➜ ORNOT ➜ WAHOO ➜ ZWIFT ➜ SPECIALIZED ➜ TREK.

Bike lights are a must-have item for anyone commuting or riding road or gravel in the winter months. Even if you already have a light, I’ve found it super useful to own an extra set to have at the office, on my other bikes, or as spares for friends.

Lezyne consistently makes great front and rear lights. While slightly pricier than budget picks found on Amazon or AliExpress, they’re durable, work well, and last several seasons. Plus, we’ve found Lezyne’s advertised runtimes and lumens are much closer to reality than many no-name lights.

Showers Pass makes our best-tested winter gloves, and they’re currently on sale at 19% off. In their review, our test rider said, “This knit, waterproof glove has a midweight feel and sufficient insulation when temperatures hover around freezing. Most riders will find the Crosspoints reach its limit at about 30-35 degrees, depending on how hard you’re riding.”.

The glove traps some body heat, so your fingers may be slightly chilly at first but will warm up within 15 minutes. Better yet, when the mercury climbs, your hands won’t feel hot and sweaty.

Electric mini-inflators burst onto the scene a couple of years ago and have rapidly become a rider favorite for pumping up your tires at home, at the trailhead, or on rides. Of the inflators we’ve tested, the RockBros model stands out for its consistency and is a favorite of Bicycling editors. It’s compact, lightweight, and has an accurate gauge. In our testing of 15 electric pumps, it inflated a road tire to 65 psi in 45 seconds, and filled five tires before running out of power.

Recent findings suggest that the Wahoo Kickr Core 2—Bicycling’s Best Overall Indoor Trainer—is on sale for the lowest price we’ve seen: $399.99. The Core combines excellent performance, great accuracy, and high max resistance in a package perfect for Zwift rides after work, winter training, and even competitive virtual racing.

Sources indicate that indoor training bikes are quickly gaining popularity for their ease of use and low maintenance. With a dedicated indoor setup, you no longer have to wrestle with getting your bike on or off the smart trainer, which also makes it convenient to share with other riders in your family. Plus, you won’t wear out pricey parts. Zwift’s Ride is our favorite: it sets up quickly and adjusts for a wide range of rider heights and fits. It also costs thousands less than its competitors.

In a recent development, shorter daylight hours and lower temps often mean fewer hours spent riding outside on the road or trail. An indoor trainer helps you maintain your fitness through the winter months while getting your riding fix. Garmin’s Tacx Flux2 is the brand’s mid-range smart trainer; with 2,000 watts of resistance, it simulates gradients up to 16%. The Flux also connects to virtual platforms like Zwift and Rouvy for immersive indoor riding experiences.

In a recent development, stainless bottles have become popular among cyclists over the past several seasons. They keep water chilled on hot rides and don’t give your water a funny plastic taste. Many gravel and off-road riders love CamelBak’s Stainless Podium, particularly for its open/closed twist-lock cap. The Podium Stainless also ranked best in our heat testing last summer and performed well in our winter bottle testing.

SUMMER BOTTLE TESTING WINTER BOTTLE TESTING.

Sources indicate that elite road and gravel helmets offer low weight, excellent ventilation, and great looks. However, those benefits usually come at a high cost. Giro’s Agilis Mips helmet is a great option if you want a pro-level look and performance without the associated price.

Industry observers note that weighing 299 grams (size medium), my Agilis is only 15 grams heavier than Giro’s premium Aries Spherical model—and the Agilis costs significantly less. The Agilis is very well-ventilated, comparable to the priciest lids on all but the hottest of rides.

This helmet features Mips technology to protect your brain from rotational forces in a crash, and Giro’s Hardbody co-molded shell to better protect it from small bumps and dings when not on your head. Plus, the Agilis uses the Roc-Loc dial system to ensure a proper fit.

Recent findings suggest that MET’s Trenta 3K Carbon is one of the top five road helmets by Virginia Tech’s helmet lab. It’s also one of the best for racing and high-performance riding, as proven by UAE Team Emirates’s results—Tour de France champion Tadej Pogačar and World Champion Brandon McNulty. While UAE riders often race the Italian brand’s Manta aero helmet, they pick the lightweight, well-ventilated Trenta 3K Carbon for climbing stages and training.

Unlike some modern helmets with similarly strong protection, the Trenta feels light and racey on your head, and almost disappears when you’re riding. The straps offer good adjustability, and the Mips Air Node liner protects without feeling bulky. However, the Trenta’s biggest drawback is its price tag. Typically priced over $500, this is an expensive piece of kit, but this deal cuts the cost by almost a third.

Arm warmers are among the most versatile pieces of cycling clothing you can own. This magical piece of kit turns your short-sleeve jersey into a long-sleeve in seconds—and you can change back to short sleeves again mid-ride if the temps rise.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve owned many pairs of arm warmers over the last three decades, and I rarely ride without them on my arms or in my jersey pocket if the temperatures are between 45 and 60 degrees. Castelli makes some of the best clothes out there, and these arm warmers are a steal for the price. They’re easy to pull on or off while riding, and they don’t sag.

Recent findings suggest that A quality rain jacket is a must-have item for riders who live anywhere it rains or snows. Rapha’s Core Rain Jacket is great option for layering over your winter jersey without adding too much bulk. It features a two-way zip for regulating body temperature, reflective hits for riding after dusk or in the early morning, and packs down small if weather clears mid-ride.

If you ride in temps below 40 degrees, a good cycling jacket is a great asset. As a Scottish brand, Endura knows a few things about riding in the cold, dark days of winter, and its MT500 Freezing Point jacket is a great option for trail rides and commuting in low temps. It features PrimaLoft Gold insulation and a DWR finish to shed rain drops. Another great feature is the MT500’s underarm zippers; they allow you to cool off and ventilate without unzipping your entire jacket.

Recent findings suggest that when cold weather hits, bib tights ensure you stay warm on rides. Of the many cycling tights available, Velocio makes some of our test editors’ favorites. The One Thermal bibs feature a soft, fleece lining and use a more relaxed, less compressive fit than some of the brands’ other options. This makes them perfect for road, gravel, and trail rides, or even layering under commuter pants.

It has been revealed that instead of shredding your nice, lightweight road tires on weather-worn winter roads, swap them out for more durable rubber. Vittoria’s Rubino tires are a proven all-season road tire with a smooth, fast-rolling center and siped edges for cornering traction. They’re tubeless-compatible, so you’ll catch fewer flats in the cold, and come in widths from 26mm to 34mm with black or tan sidewalls.

Sources indicate that modern bike computers do much more than display speed and distance. These devices are a critical information hub for many cyclists. Cycling computers can record ride metrics, display real-time performance data, and help you navigate—but that’s only scratching the surface of their capabilities.

It has been revealed that the Elemnt Bolt 3 is Wahoo’s tiny-but-mighty cycling-specific computer. Wahoo equips it with a 2.3-inch high-resolution screen, up to 20 hours of battery life, and integration with Strava, Komoot, and other popular cycling platforms.

Recent findings suggest that another great option is the Hammerhead Karoo. This head unit features a 3.2-inch color touchscreen Gorilla Glass display and up to 35 hours of run time. The Karoo stands out for its mapping and navigation. The navigation, combined with its pop-up hill climb feature and ability to sideload apps, makes the Karoo my overall favorite.

POC makes comfortable, well-ventilated helmets for road, gravel, and mountain biking. The Kortal is a trail-style helmet, featuring an adjustable visor, room to stow your glasses or goggles, and plenty of airflow for hot summer trail rides. The straps are also comfortable, something that often bugs me on other lids.

Recent findings suggest that fresh bar tape is the quickest and most cost-effective way to improve the look, feel, and comfort of any road or gravel bike. I’ve used Fizik tape on several bikes that have come in for testing, and have also bought it for my personal bikes. It has enough cushion, reliable grip, and is easy to wrap. You can’t ask for much more from bar tape.

While many riders are adding electric mini-inflators to their tool kits, a quality floor pump remains an essential part of every cyclist’s arsenal. They never run out of batteries, pump as many tires as your arms can handle, and are easy to use.

Industry observers note that riders and mechanics have trusted Topeak’s JoeBlow pumps for decades—because they work. Although many JoeBlow models are low-cost and utilitarian, the JoeBlow Ace DX is a Cadillac-level floor pump. It features alloy construction with a metal chuck and can inflate tires up to 260 psi, with three different inflation modes: high-volume, standard, or high-pressure.

#125601. What’s the Minimum Amount of Mileage You Can Do to Maintain Fitness? Experts Answer

What’s the Minimum Amount of Mileage You Can Do to Maintain Fitness? Experts Answer

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1365 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for some runners, taking a week or two off from running after a race is the hard part—they can’t wait to ramp back up their volume again.
  • Still, if you trained for months to build up the fitness, including your aerobic capacity, lactate threshold, and running economy, you probably want to try to maintain at least some of that afterward.
  • Maintenance mode also gives you the flexibility to be able to jump into a 10K or half-marathon on a whim, notes Mike Sheehy, running coach for Team Abbott who has completed more than 100 marathons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for some runners, taking a week or two off from running after a race is the hard part—they can’t wait to ramp back up their volume again. But for others, crossing a finish line (of any distance) might feel like a natural point to take a break from the sport, or at least to significantly scale back.

Still, if you trained for months to build up the fitness, including your aerobic capacity, lactate threshold, and running economy, you probably want to try to maintain at least some of that afterward. That way, you can go into a spring training cycle with a solid base.

Maintenance mode also gives you the flexibility to be able to jump into a 10K or half-marathon on a whim, notes Mike Sheehy, running coach for Team Abbott who has completed more than 100 marathons.

According to recent reports, keeping a steady mileage base also allows you to experiment. “This gives you a chance to try upcoming fuels, try new gear, a new pair of shorts, new pair of shoes, stuff you didn't like during your block,” Sheehy says. You could also experiment with pace. “This is a great block to think about moving your easy pace up 15 seconds to let your heart and body start adapting to that new norm.”.

It has been revealed that if you want to strike a balance between giving yourself a well-deserved break and completely reversing all of your gains, the question becomes: What’s the minimum running you can do to maintain your fitness? And how long can I do that without falling back?

Here’s what running coaches and an exercise physiologist have to say, plus what other forms of exercise come into play in the maintenance phase.

GET YOUR MAINTENANCE LOOKS HERE.

First, it’s key to note that taking a week or two off after a marathon and at least one week for the half is not only encouraged, it’s probably the best thing you can do for your body—and your mind.

“The thing I encourage all my runners to remember is patience,” states Sheehy. “Let your body heal and take that time.” He typically advises runners to take a full week off, then slowly add in easy miles without rushing to get back to quality workouts.

It has been revealed that then by the end of week two, you enter the true maintenance phase. “This is really an exciting time of running,” Sheehy indicates. “This is where we’re keeping 90 percent of the fitness with about 60 percent of the work.” He recommends taking the average mileage from your peak marathon training weeks rather than the single highest weekly mileage.

It has been revealed that this tends to net out to between 20 and 30 miles a week in the maintenance phase for marathon runners and 10 to 15 miles a week for half-marathoners. That might look like three shorter, easier runs during the week and an 8- to 12-miler on the weekend. (Experts agree it’s best to run more frequently at lower volume for each run than do fewer, longer runs.) “That keeps you 90 percent fit, but allows you to enjoy running and not have the pressure of having to run six or five days a week and without having structured workouts,” Sheehy notes.

Andrew M. Jones, Ph.D., professor of applied physiology at the University of Exeter in the U.K., puts the minimum effective dose of maintenance running slightly lower—at 50 percent—though after about four to six weeks at half the volume, runners will likely start to see “more significant deterioration,” he indicates, specifically of race-specific endurance. (Running economy may be more resilient.).

That’s not necessarily a bad thing (and allows you to focus on other goals; more on this soon), and 50 percent is enough to preserve a foundation to allow you to pick up at the beginning of a 16-week marathon training strategy with relative ease.

It has been revealed that greg Laraia, a running coach at Motiv in Upcoming York City, agrees and provides this example: Say a runner finished Berlin on September 27 and aims to run London on April 24. After time off, he’d have them work back up to 50 percent of their mileage by October 25, then hover in the 50 to 60 percent of mileage range until early January when their London block would start in earnest.

Retaining intensity during the maintenance phase is arguably more important than frequency and duration, per Jones. “It’s impossible to give a minimum effective dose [for intensity] but ideally by week two [after a marathon] they’d get back to the pre-marathon training intensity but with lower volume,” he states, which might be lower duration and/or frequency of quality running. “Intensity is the key stimulus.”.

To hit this stimulus, Sheehy and Laraia both like to have runners add in strides (e.g., four to six 30- to 60-second strides as part of an easy run) before doing more intense speed workouts that could make their way back into the weekly schedule about a month after a race.

Sheehy provides an example of a speed workout he likes to include during the maintenance phase:.

“The fresh race pace is something I know they can achieve that is apparent in previous race results and workouts; not some aspirational wish pace,” Sheehy says. “This will give them the confidence they need or maybe a wake up call, but it makes for a great starting point, and allows us to calibrate their easy paces and use the lower volumes to let their body (and heart) adjust to the new norm.”.

Industry observers note that sheehy cautions against swapping out runs that make up your maintenance mileage for other cardio, as it is important to maintain the specificity of running if you want to maintain running fitness. But he often adds in an indoor cycling day during his offseason on top of four or so days of running. If you dropped down your running frequency, an aerobic cross-training workout can support your fitness maintenance. Plus, it gives you a mental break, Jones says.

Laraia says one case where swapping maintenance miles for other cardio could make sense would be when runners come off a fall race injured or worn down and simply need a break from running so much. “Running is always going to be the best option because running is the sport, but if an elliptical or a bike is going to make you miss [running] enough to want to do it again, let’s start there,” he says.

The maintenance phase is also a great time to focus on strength training, Jones states. Sheehy agrees, suggesting aiming for two to three days a week. You can do more volume (either via an extra day or more sets/reps) during this phase, but it’s still vital to include one true rest day in your proposal, Sheehy says.

Strength work helps to build neuromuscular capacity, improve power that can translate to speed, and strengthen your tendons and ligaments for the upcoming season, especially if you focus on heavier lifting. “Let’s get comfortable with the extra load and then let’s see if it makes running better and more efficient,” Laraia says.

GET YOUR STRENGTH WORKOUTS HERE.

Laraia indicates signs that you may have pulled back too much include a higher-than-usual heart rate during runs or paces that feel harder than normal.

It has been revealed that still, it’s probably better to lose a little bit more running fitness in the offseason than to push yourself too hard, he notes. The former is going to put you in a better position to start a fresh training block in the spring, compared with the latter, which could lead to burnout and could set your next training cycle back.

“Realistically, you’re going to be better off taking the extra day versus trying to push through something if you’re early in a block or just trying to maintain fitness,” Laraia notes. “I’d rather you be 100 percent recovered for every run versus in the build,” where it might make sense to go into a run feeling a little depleted.

Garmin LiveTrack Now Alerts Waze Drivers to Nearby Cyclists

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rearview radars are one of our favorite cycling accessories because they alert riders when a vehicle is approaching from behind.
  • It has been revealed that here’s how it works.
  • Waze indicates the alert comes when a cyclist gets closer, but it hasn’t specified the distance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rearview radars are one of our favorite cycling accessories because they alert riders when a vehicle is approaching from behind. Now Garmin and Waze are flipping that warning around: Their upcoming partnership alerts drivers when a cyclist using Garmin’s LiveTrack is nearby.

It has been revealed that here’s how it works. Start an outdoor cycling activity with LiveTrack on a compatible Garmin Edge computer or smartwatch, and your location will appear in Waze as a moving cyclist icon. Drivers don’t need to be navigating a route to see cyclists; Waze told me the icons appear whenever the app is open, as riders enter the driver’s broader route area or immediate surroundings.

Waze indicates the alert comes when a cyclist gets closer, but it hasn’t specified the distance. In an email response to my questions, Garmin told me alerts go to “relevant drivers,” usually when the rider and driver are on the same road and traveling in the same direction. A cyclist farther ahead on the driver’s mapped route may also trigger one.

In a recent development, if several riders are together, Waze demonstrates one icon to avoid repeat alerts. If they spread out, multiple icons appear. Garmin describes the grouping feature as “built-in clustering logic.”.

For Waze users, cyclist alerts are on by default but can be turned off in the app’s settings. Riders opt in to Waze sharing through Garmin, but only once. After that, sharing starts whenever they begin a cycling LiveTrack, whether they start it manually or set it to start automatically.

Garmin states any Edge computer or smartwatch with LiveTrack is compatible. LiveTrack requires a phone paired with Garmin Connect and cellular coverage; Garmin’s LTE-enabled devices can run LiveTrack without relying on the phone’s connection.

No additional subscription or purchase is required. Waze indicates drivers see only a temporary alert that a cyclist is nearby, not the rider’s name, identity, or exact route. Sharing stops when the ride ends.

This is not V2X, the connected-vehicle technology that has been simmering in the background. V2X systems let vehicles exchange information with one another, roadside infrastructure, and other road consumers, including cyclists. Garmin and Waze are taking an app-based route to a similar goal: LiveTrack sends a rider’s location to Waze, which can alert drivers using the app.

Sources indicate that it’s a sensible idea, but it requires the latest apps and firmware, a Garmin rider who has opted in, a working connection, and a driver using Waze. It isn’t a substitute for cycling-friendly infrastructure, and it won’t fix distracted drivers or jerks in cars. But reminding drivers that cyclists are on the road is a step in the right direction.

Would you enable Waze sharing for your LiveTrack rides? If you use Waze while driving, would a cyclist icon or alert change how you approach the road? Tell us in the comments, or join me on Discord. I’d especially like to hear from riders who already use LiveTrack or Waze: What would you want to know before turning this on?

Sources indicate that A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.
