#125581. The 12 Best Carbon Plate Shoes for Setting PRs, Running Your First Marathon, and Crossing the Finish Line Upright

📅 07 Jun 2023 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3932 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

The 12 Best Carbon Plate Shoes for Setting PRs, Running Your First Marathon, and Crossing the Finish Line Upright

📅 07 Jun 2023 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3932 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Sources indicate that there are several max-cushioned shoes we recommend to carry you through hours of pounding pavement, but the true titans—composed of super foams sandwiching carbon-fiber plates—are listed here.
  • In 2017, Nike shook up running as we knew it with the unveiling of its Vaporfly 4%, a carbon plate marathon racing shoe that promised a 4 percent improvement in running economy (the measure of how fast you run based on the level of oxygen you use).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that there are several max-cushioned shoes we recommend to carry you through hours of pounding pavement, but the true titans—composed of super foams sandwiching carbon-fiber plates—are listed here. There’s also a slew of latest super shoes that made their debut this marathon cycle. We’ll update accordingly once these racers are available.

In 2017, Nike shook up running as we knew it with the unveiling of its Vaporfly 4%, a carbon plate marathon racing shoe that promised a 4 percent improvement in running economy (the measure of how fast you run based on the level of oxygen you use). Today, almost every shoe brand has a super shoe with a carbon plate and super foams, and they all make the same promise as the Vaporfly 4%: less energy expenditure while racing, or the ability to run faster with the same effort.

In a recent development, here, we list the top performers based on wear-tester feedback and our own experiences racing in them. And if you’re in the market for other shoes to help you with your training, we have a buying guide for those too.

Your first marathon → Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 (Men’s/Women’s)For a PR → Nike Alphafly 4 (Men’s/Women’s)But want to train in a plated shoe → New Balance SC Rebel (Men’s/Women’s)A flat and fast course → Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 (Unisex)A half marathon → Asics Metaspeed Edge Tokyo (Unisex)And want to try low drop → Altra Vanish Carbon 3 (Men’s/Women’s)And need support → Saucony Endorphin Pro 5 (Men’s/Women’s)And have wide feet → Hoka Cielo X1 3.0 (Unisex)On a track → Puma Fast-R Nitro Elite 3 (Men’s/Women’s)A 5K or 10K → New Balance SuperComp Elite v6 (Men’s/Women’s)On a trail → Hoka Tecton X 4 (Men’s/Women’s)An ultra → On Cloudultra Pro (Men’s/Women’s).

According to recent reports, besides our local testers, some of whom have been testing for us for the past 15 years, and staff who’ve also logged their share of road and trail time in these shoes, I have tested several of these shoes on race days. I have run 28 marathons since 2010, including 14 consecutive Boston Marathons. And I have made the split-second decision to race in latest shoes marathon morning.

I’ve spoken with brand shoe development teams and have kept up with the latest super shoe releases. Fresh shoes not listed here are still undergoing the testing process and will be added once feedback is in.

All of the shoes on this list were tested by local runners and Runner’s World staff. Our local testers include 300-plus men and women of various running experience levels, paces, arch heights, and gait patterns. From enthusiasts who run for fun to several Olympic-qualifying hopefuls, our mix of testers rounds out a sample of the overall running pop.

RW editors, including myself, have also raced in these shoes, from 5K to marathon distance (and some ultrarunners). We take into consideration fit, feel, and ride to determine the best racing shoes for almost every kind of runner hoping to PR, or just enjoy the propulsive experience of running on carbon plates sandwiched between super foams.

Recent findings suggest that on a plane, running a shakeout run, and anytime a marathon was weeks away or days past, I’d hear first-timers and seasoned vets say the Adizero Adios Pro 4 was their race day shoe of choice. The latest iteration is sure to have the same mentions next race cycle.

I didn’t have the chance to race in the Adizero Adios Pro 5 yet, but I did try them out on my usual Central Park circuit in Upcoming York City. I was practically racing my casual loop after slurping half a can of beer (it was a long day on the job). It obviously wasn’t the kiwi-flavored Belgian White that had me clocking marathon pace (it got kinda funky after the 25th sip).

Industry observers note that the carbon rim, which replaces the 4’s energy rods, is the secret sauce that subtracts weights and encourages a powerful snap that had me run up and down Harlem Hill like a gazelle. The Lightstrike Pro foam is also slightly firmer, which helps with high rebound and stability.

It has been revealed that my only knock is how the rim shreds the hell of my ankle if my form gets slow and sloppy. But it’s a character trait. Senior Art Director Colin McSherry, for instance, ran his first marathon and had no complications—shoe- or first 26.2-related—during his run.

Shop Men’s at adidas.com | Shop Women’s at adidas.com.

Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 Review.

The Alphafly 3 went through some major changes to become more inclusive in terms of fit, weight, and ride. How do you update a shoe that was worn by the late Kelvin Kiptum, former marathon world record holder (2:00:35)? It starts with the Air units.

Industry observers note that the ones in the Alphafly 4 are lighter and softer. During his testing, Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate noted how the unit visibly squishes down when you stomp on the forefoot. The effect is a smoother, comfier ride with lots of pop.

It has been revealed that the width of the shoe is also slightly wider (Nike really wants runners to stop saying their shoes are too unstable and narrow). Dengate noted how he didn’t have to slow down when turning corners.

Industry observers note that the main critique is that loud clomping sound. But at this point—is it really an Alphafly if you can’t hear it coming up from behind you meters away?

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

According to recent reports, the jury is still out on the pros and cons of solely training in super shoes, but we’re in the camp of keeping your special trainer fresh for race day. You can get a couple of runs in to troubleshoot and see if there are any challenges pre-marathon or half, but I still urge runners to save the magic. But if you can’t get enough of that super foam, carbon plate high, enter the SC Rebel.

Latest Balance created this shoe specifically to make your training feel easier. It has the brand’s new TPEE-based Infinion foam, tuned for power runs, just like the SuperComp Elite v6 (New Balance’s premium racing shoe). It’s also an ideal alternative for racing if you need more stability. The shoe has a broader platform and grippy outsole that kept me upright on wet mud during a long run.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

Newly introduced Balance SuperComp Rebel Review.

It has been revealed that the Endorphin Elite 3 is as squishy and bouncy as its predecessor, but Saucony made the shoe more stable by connecting the forefoot and heel. Turns are less scary, but there’s still a learning curve to master the incredible energy return running in these shoes.

I tested them at a 5K and 3K in the Brooklyn Navy Yard, which was pocked with potholes and patched with slippery gravel. The shoes cut corners, but I still felt the need to slow down—or wipe out. I think on a more controlled runner’s feet these would make her feel powerful and unbeatable.

The source of that aggressive bounce is the TPEE-based IncrediRun foam. Its ride rivals even PEBA’s energy return.

It has been revealed that the shoe also didn’t produce hot spots in the toe area. Saucony seems to have improved the fit with the third version. Once I wield this shoe’s power I won’t be afraid to run longer than a 10K. No friction here.

Shop Endorphin Elite 3 at saucony.com.

Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 Review.

It has been revealed that when I ran the Tokyo Marathon last year, I laced up in the Asics Metaspeed Sky Paris because I wanted more cushioning in the forefoot area. Asics recognized there are two ways of racing: stride running or cadence running. The Sky is intended for stride running: when you have a more powerful gait with longer strides and tend to strike on the midfoot.

At the Sydney Marathon this year, I opted for the Metaspeed Edge Tokyo instead. I felt the Edge would give me the, er, competitive edge, so to speak. My steps per minute are usually more than the average runner due to my mechanics and, well, because I’m short. The shoe has a scooped plate tilted slightly downward to cater to those with shorter steps (cadence running). I ended up hitting my sub-3:10 goal, finishing in 3:05.

Industry observers note that the Edge Tokyo is updated with a softer underfoot, making the shoe more flexible. This makes the shoe have an incredible snap at toe-off. I was able to change gears at a fast clip when I latched onto a runner I was determined to pass (not always the best race strategy, but worked like a charm when I saw male runners try to overtake me).

It has been revealed that where competitors’ shoes have “air pods” or decoupled heels, the Metaspeeds provide runners with a simplified, choose-your-own-adventure super shoe that packs a powerful punch. One note for the wise: Because the Edge Tokyo has less firm cushioning, my heels and arches felt sore postrace. If you have heavy footfalls like me, have those recovery sandals waiting for you at bag check.

Shop Asics Metaspeed Edge Tokyo at amazon.com.

Asics Metaspeed Tokyo Shoes Review.

Altra started its journey into super shoes by staying true to itself. The Vanish Carbon 1 and 2 had wide toeboxes and were zero drop. But the Altra team knew there would have to be a compromise to go up against competitors’ shoes: the Vanish Carbon 3 needed a drop. The brand preserved the Altra way by adding just 4 mm (like the shoes in its Experience collection) to the heel with an aggressive rocker profile to promote propulsion.

Another Altra signature in the shoe is the roomy toebox that gives racers space to splay their toes, allowing them to engage their digits and power up during push-off.

It has been revealed that the third iteration has pure PEBA midsole foam called FastRce. The foam provides more energy return and 2.6 percent improved running economy over the Vanish Carbon 2, which had a PEBA/EVA blend in its midsole.

The overall package presents a racer capable of racing against the other super shoes on this list.

Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com.

The Endorphin Pro 5 has a more stable ride than its springier sibling, the Endorphin Elite 2, which we also included on this list.

Recent findings suggest that its midsole is dual-layer PEBA, with one layer Pwrrun PB and the other layer Pwrrun HG. These layers provide a high-rebound ride and work with the rocker Speedroll tech to encourage fast, smooth turnover.

Testers like the shoe’s propulsive ride as well as support throughout their workouts.

Industry observers note that “What stood out most was the combination of propulsion and stability,” noted tester Srah Pezzino. “The carbon plate paired with Saucony’s Pwrrun HG foam delivers a responsive, fast ride without feeling unstable or overly bouncy. This helped immensely during longer tempo runs when fatigue starts to creep in. I felt like the shoe encouraged good mechanics and smooth turnover rather than forcing speed.

“Compared to previous carbon-plated shoes I’ve worn, the Pro 5 feels more predictable and controlled, especially when my form isn’t perfect late in a run. It’s a shoe that makes you feel fast without punishing you for not being perfectly locked in.”.

Shop Men’s at saucony.com | Shop Women’s at saucony.com.

According to recent reports, the lightest Hoka marathon racing shoe yet is the Cielo X1 3.0, with street cred at the 2025 Chicago Marathon. Hoka-sponsored pro-runner Alex Masai raced in a blacked-out prototype of the shoe, shaved nearly four minutes off his personal best time, and podiumed third with a 2:04:37 finish.

And our testers clocked the shoe’s massive updates, as well. “The 3.0 is sturdier than the 2.0,” said tester Mike Browne. “I’m referring to the sturdiness mainly on heel strikes. I wore the 2.0 during marathon training and in a marathon, and they actually underpronated a little. I think that is what caused the outside heel rubber to come off on both shoes. The 3.0 has corrected that matter and seems to strike the ground in the center, which makes for a more even wear on the shoe.”.

Besides implementing a lighter upper, the Hoka team redesigned the midsole shape, creating a long channel that runs down the center of the shoe. The rocker also isn’t as exaggerated. What you get is a more stable, smoother ride while racing with propulsion that’s comparable to Hoka’s competitors’. The fit is also broader in the midfoot, making the Cielo X1 3.0 a good choice for runners with wide feet.

Shop Hoka Cielo X1 3 at hoka.com.

The Fast-R Nitro Elite 3 is a prime pick for marathon racing, but it’s also a solid choice for everything else under 26.2 miles. The shoe is so lightweight and delivers such explosive rebound—“you feel like you’re running straight down a trampoline,” indicates a tester—that it left some of us feeling like we had brownie batter for legs after hard efforts.

The shoe was the talk of the industry prelaunch after Puma released a study (which the brand sponsored) comparing the Fast-R Nitro Elite 3’s performance to the Nike Alphafly 3, Adidas Adios Pro Evo 1, and Puma Fast-R 2. The study claimed the Elite 3 was 3.15 to 3.62 percent more economical than its competitors.

Industry observers note that putting those numbers aside, our testers agreed this is one powerful racing shoe. “The foam used in this shoe is very noticeable, even when simply starting with a short warmup in the shoe,” says tester Codi Januszkiewicz, who compares the ride to the Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 4. “Accelerating from a warmup pace straight into some speedwork intervals felt smooth; somehow moving faster in this shoe felt even easier than the warmup.”.

In a recent development, but that power is a lot to handle. “The stability is lacking,” says tester Sean O’Connor. “Almost felt high heelish to me, and it jacked up my calves and feet a little as well. When I ran in them it felt like I was perpetually holding onto the shoe with my feet. I think that's why it made my calves and feet sore.”.

Some can handle the shoe’s intensity over a long period of time. Others may assign the Elite 3 as their mid-distance racing shoe instead. I wore the Elite 3 at a Trackmith 5000 meters over the summer, hitting a PR at 19:12. It’s cush in the heel, but judging by my footfalls, which are heavy, I think racing them in a 26.2 would prolong my usual recovery time postrun.

When I raced the 2025 London Marathon, I had been training in the FuelCell SuperComp Elite v4 but instead opted for the FuelCell SuperComp Pacer v2. The Pacer is sleeker and lightweight, unlike the SuperComp Elite v4, which was too beefy for my small frame. The SuperComp Elite v6 is the version of the shoe I would have raced in. Unfortunately, I can’t go back to April 2025. Fortunately for you, the Elite v6 is here just in time for fall marathon season.

Sources indicate that the shoe features the brand’s Infinion foam, which was introduced in the 1080v15. The Elite v6’s version of the TPEE- and TPU-based foam is dialed-in for race-ready energy return.

Industry observers note that I took the shoe out on a track for a 2 x 2-mile workout at 6:45 pace and the shoes handled turns and helped me hit goal pace. The ride isn’t as aggressive as the Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 or Alphafly, and the cushioning is firmer. Runners with an efficient stride and good form can get away with running marathons and halfs in these shoes, but I’d recommend these for 5Ks and 10Ks because of the firmness and less explosive rebound. The lighter weight makes it ideal for track and medium-distance road races.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

Upcoming Balance SuperComp Elite v6 Review.

In a recent development, though I’ve been racing for 20 years, nothing will get me running an ultra on the trail—which is where our Senior Editor Cat Bowen comes in. Bowen conquered scrambles on steep climbs, dusty ridgelines, gnarly technical trails, and more types of terrain than I run in a year, while testing the long-awaited Tecton X 4.

She gave a shoutout to the hardy Matryx upper that’s “tough as nails” and the grippy 4mm lugs that prevented her from plunging forward. The plus/minus with the shoe is that built-in gaiter collar. Bowen appreciated the extra coverage, but lamented how difficult it was to put on the shoe (we get it: a side zipper would be a good cheat but adds weight). “There is absolutely no reason why this shoe has a front pull tab and nothing in the back,” she wrote in her review.

Still, the fresh cushioning, Hoka’s ProFly X, and non-winged plate make for a more energized ride that’s less rigid without losing stability. It’s a great shoe for unpredictable. but Bowen urges you to not go the no-sock route.

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com.

Sources indicate that for hours, days, weeks on the trail, there’s the Cloudultra Pro. Bowen has gone through three pairs of the shoe—not because they lack durability but because she likes them so much and runs that much—and appreciates how she doesn’t have to slice the sides. Feet swell during ultras, but it sounds like On prepared for that with its roomy but secure upper.

Sources indicate that another plus in Bowen’s column of ultra shoe musts is the Cloudultra Pro’s lateral stability. Maneuvering over rugged, uneven terrain could spell twisted ankles and slipping and sliding, but the shoe didn’t lead Bowen astray.

Ultrarunner Pat Heine-Holmberg also wore the shoe around Germany’s Zugspitze, where he raced the 102-mile ZUT1000 and ran on “every surface imaginable.”.

Shop Men’s at on.com | Shop Women’s at on.com.

Brands are now beginning to release carbon shoes in men’s and women’s sizes. Still, in some cases there’s not much difference between the types of shoes except for maybe the sizing and colors. If the shoes are unisex, it may take a few try-ons to get the fit right. In my unisex racing shoe experience, I’ve found the collar can be loose while the midfoot can be tight. You may want to size up or down, and adopt the heel-lock tying method if the heel area feels too loose.

Do all carbon-fiber plates behave the same way? Sort of. An notable lesson to learn here is that the plate isn’t the secret sauce of super shoes—it doesn’t cause propulsion. Instead, the plate, sandwiched between the highly responsive foams, acts as a stabilizer to the super foam. This is why super shoes have such tall stack heights, and why World Athletics caps racing shoe stack height at 40 mm. The super foam—and amount underfoot—is a major advantage.

When choosing a carbon-plate shoe, you’ll want to consider what you’re using it for—racing on the road or trail—and, if possible, have your gait evaluated to determine the best plate angle if you’re looking at shoes specific to running type.

In a recent development, some plates are full-length or have cutouts. In shoes like the Asics Metaspeed Edge and Metaspeed Sky, the plate’s angle differentiates running types. The Edge’s plate dips lower in the forefoot so cadence runners can roll off their toes faster. The Sky’s plate sits flat in the forefoot, allowing stride runners to leverage bounce on longer steps.

In a recent development, the secret sauce in super shoes is the foam. PEBA (polyether block amide) was once considered the holy grail of all foams and you can still find it in most super shoes, but newer models are using TPEE (thermoplastic polyester elastomer) and A-TPU (aliphatic thermoplastic polyurethane) because they’re more resistant to bottoming out, or going flat. The ride is more durable—and can be quite aggressively bouncy and squishy.

To truly gauge which foam is best for you, trying on the shoe and giving it a run (preferably with some cornering) will help you determine if you want a firmer or squishier ride.

Industry observers note that A carbon-fiber plate shoe is an investment, costing anywhere from $240 upward of $500. There are a couple of things to take into account on a personal level before buying: Can you afford a trainer that’s less durable compared to the standard workhorse shoe, which lasts between 450 to 500 miles?

Sources indicate that while these super shoes are more durable than the ones made eight years ago, they still have a shorter shelf life due to high-performance foams—PEBA and supercritical blends—wearing down faster. Lastly, is the return there? While brands claim these shoes can improve performance, it’s not guaranteed your running economy will improve by around 4 percent.

I spoke with Ted Fitzpatrick, Saucony’s VP of product management, about the differences. He made these key points between carbon and nylon plates:.

It has been revealed that A nylon plate is semirigid with some flexibility. A carbon plate is rigid with little or no flexibility. Popsicle analogy—Imagine the plate as the stick that holds the soft ice cream together. The fundamental use of the plates is to keep the dimensional stability of the foam. With each type of plate, each offers different levels of compliance. The plate maintains the forward rolling effect of super shoes. Carbon is the stiffest, which offers the most concentrated effect of speed roll technology. Nylon still adds stiffness, however, it offers better compliance in how the foot transitions in the gait cycle. Some individuals can respond better to different plates. It is down to what works best for the user.

Saucony offers the nylon-plated Endorphin Speed 6, a training shoe that complements its racer, the Endorphin Pro. The shoe can also serve as a more affordable racing shoe, at $180. (The Endorphin Elite 3 and Endorphin Pro 5 cost $290 and $240.).

According to recent reports, “The foam is what does the heavy lifting of a super shoe, however it’s the plate that guides how each foam behaves to the user,” says Fitzpatrick. “It is best to train in both to strengthen and build ‘muscle memory’ into different muscle groups.”.

According to recent reports, however, we wouldn’t recommend solely training in super shoes. For one thing, it would be extremely expensive to use these shoes as daily trainers when they have a shorter shelf life compared to standard everyday shoes. We advise going on a couple of runs before racing in the shoes, to get used to running in them and check for hot spots. While running constantly in these shoes won’t necessarily lead to injury, overuse and the desire to run faster in carbon shoes will likely lead to getting sidelined if you’re not careful.

Industry observers note that amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

#125580. Tech Report: The Unexpected Benefits of Doing Inversions in Yoga

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1469 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Yogajournal ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: The Unexpected Benefits of Doing Inversions in Yoga

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1469 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • (Photo: Andrew Clark | Design in Canva by Laura Harold).
  • According to recent reports, in Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975.
  • The Headstand and Shoulderstand positions, Sirsasana and Sarvangasana, have long been known as the king and queen of the asanas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Andrew Clark | Design in Canva by Laura Harold).

According to recent reports, in Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about the effects of inversions in yoga first appeared in the November-December 1983 concern of Yoga Journal. You can find more of our Archives here. You can also read more about inversions.

The Headstand and Shoulderstand positions, Sirsasana and Sarvangasana, have long been known as the king and queen of the asanas. By reversing the body’s usual relationship to gravity, these asanas produce numerous beneficial changes in the body’s physiological systems. Because there are also many additional physical, psychological, and emotional benefits that come with the practice of these poses, they are often considered the core of a complete asana practice. However, to truly experience their benefits and prevent injury, they must be done correctly.

What are the effects of reversing the gravitational pull on the human body and why is it desirable? Are there dangers and precautions to working with inversions, and what are the safest ways to work with gravity? These are questions all of us may have asked, and with the recent backlash against inversions, they deserve a full discussion.

All posture and movement must take into account the constant downward pulling force of gravity. Our bones provide some support and resistance, but fluids, which compromise 75 to 80 percent of our mass, are at the mercy of the “major G.” Just as water always flows downhill, the liquids in our body flow down the gravitational gradient, and the circulatory system must constantly adjust to gravity’s effects.

According to recent reports, in “Effects of Inverted Poses on Cardiovascular Physiology,” IYTE Review, Vol. 3, #3, Marcia Stefanick, Ph.D., details these adjustments. As the body changes its relationship to gravity, she writes, “profound changes occur in the distribution of blood in the vessels and the return of blood to the heart, as well as in the heart rate and blood pressure.” The cardiovascular system is composed of the heart and blood vessels. The heart consists of two separate pumps. One pumps blood into the lungs where carbon dioxide is exchanged for oxygen. This fresh blood returns to the heart and the second pump squeezes it out to the body.

The blood flows outward through large vessels known as arteries, which in turn branch and subdivide into the smaller and smaller vessels that wind their way to every organ and tissue in the body. At the level of the smallest vessels, the capillaries, the oxygen and other nutrients and messengers leave the blood stream and are transported to the cells. At the same time, carbon dioxide and other metabolic wastes are absorbed into the blood stream. This deoxygenated blood flows from the capillaries into larger vessels (venules), which lead to the still larger veins that return the blood to the heart, where the cycle begins again.

In a recent development, because some of the unwanted cell waste material is too large to be absorbed through the tiny pores in the walls of the capillaries, a second set of vessels, the lymphatic system, transports excess cellular fluid as well as large protein molecules, dead cell matter, bacteria and other material. Before being recycled back into the blood stream near the heart, this fluid is filtered by the lymph nodes, which are located at critical junctures along the lymphatic system network. At these points, dead cells and particles are absorbed, bacteria are attacked and digested, and toxins are neutralized. Thus, the lymphatic system plays a key role in guarding the body against infection and in maintaining overall health.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most important functions of the cardiovascular system is to deliver fresh blood to the brain. In lying-down positions, the heart is at the same level as the brain, and gravity has a minor effect on the movement of blood between these two organs. In sitting or standing, however, the brain is obviously above the heart and the heart muscle must work intensely to pump against the pull of gravity. In an inverted position, the brain is below the level of the heart and gravity pulls blood into the brain. In these positions, the brain receives the proper blood supply with the minimum effort of the heart.

Sources indicate that tests done by Shanker Rao, as described in Science Studies Yoga by James Funderburk, show how the heart rate varies with gravity. His subjects, medical students with some experience in yoga, exhibited an average heart rate of 67 beats per minute in the supine position, rising to 84 beats per minute upon standing. In the Headstand position, these subjects displayed a 69 beats-per-minute average. This heart rate variation was accomplished by a variation in fluid pressure in the arteries, veins, glands and organs. The regular increase in pressure in the head, neck and chest regions brought about by inversions maintains the elasticity of the vessels and tissues, and it is this elasticity that is a key factor in maintaining health.

In a recent development, just as it affects arterial blood flow, gravity affects the flow of venous blood back to the heart. There are three ways in which the deoxygenated blood can be returned to the heart. The first is gravity, which will drain the region above the heart of the venous blood and lymphatic fluid, but will resist the return of fluids from the lower body. The second two mechanisms, the respiratory pump and the skeletal musculature, must do all the work of returning the fluids below the heart. The changing pressure in the thoracic cavity, which pulls air into the lungs, pulls fluids toward the heart. Exhalations are quite notable in this respiratory pumping action. Also, the contraction and releasing of the skeletal muscles serve to pump the venous and lymphatic fluids through their respective vessels. These vessels are equipped with a series of one-way valves that allow blood to flow toward the heart only, thus preventing backflow.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, these two mechanisms cannot compete against gravity for long periods of time. During the course of a typical day, most humans will spend 16 or more hours with the head above the heart and the legs and the pelvic area below. Thus, gravity has a negative effect on the venous and lymphatic return from most of the body, and if the muscles of the legs are not continuously contracting and releasing, fluid begins to accumulate in the lower body. This will almost always occur where there is not much opportunity for movement.

According to recent reports, because the veins and lymphatic vessels are quite elastic, they can expand to hold large quantities of fluid, but, if not given periodic relief from this pooling, the vessels eventually lose their resilience to become permanently distended. The one-way valves then break down from over-stretching and varicose veins result. (Inversions can alleviate the problems of varicose veins, and, if begun in time, can prevent them.) Periodic inversions allow gravity to drain the lower body, relieving pressure and recycling the lymphatic fluid and venous blood. This in turn gives the cells a continuous supply of fresh nutrients and cleanses them of metabolic wastes. An efficient circulatory system, so notable to health, is thus maintained and improved by inversions.

Sources indicate that as we have seen, there are many tremendous benefits to be gained by inverting the body. However, it is equally important to be aware of the potential dangers involved in inverted positions. Needless to say, everyone should check with their before beginning any physical regimen. Furthermore, it is always wise to be cautious and work into things slowly.

Certain groups of people should avoid all inversions except when working under the most expert guidance. Those with high blood pressure are one such group, since the cardiovascular changes of inversions are potentially damaging to them. Under the supervision of a physician or an experienced yoga teacher, some people with high blood pressure may be able to do some inversions, but this is not an area to be explored by the average student or teacher. Other people who should avoid inversions are those who experience certain eye conditions—such as glaucoma or detached retina—hiatal hernia, heart or stroke problems, epilepsy, seizures or other brain disorders, and spinal injury (except when inversions are used as part of a supervised therapy program).

Sources indicate that certain temporary conditions also prohibit the practice of inversions. People are advised not to practice inversions during the menstrual period, and inversions during pregnancy should be practiced only by experienced students working with an experienced teacher. Active inversions should also be avoided by older people with osteoporosis, especially those with a history of vertebral fractures.

#125579. Is Your AI Strength Strategy Wasting Your Time? A Coach Weighs In

Is Your AI Strength Strategy Wasting Your Time? A Coach Weighs In

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1343 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s not uncommon nowadays to ask AI to write your grocery list, design your kid’s birthday party invitation, and advise you on how best to taper before your next race, so we’re fairly certain there are a few triathletes out there asking Claude or Chat to draft a strength training program too.
  • Before you decide to do the same (or perhaps it’s too late and you already have), we thought we’d run an AI experiment where we ask a real human strength coach to assess the bot’s work to help decide how much of the plan is helpful for a multisport athlete, and how much would be a waste of time.
  • We asked ChatGPT for a strength routine suitable for a triathlete, and about four seconds later it returned a two-day blueprint complete with sets and reps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Brad Kaminski/Triathlete).

It’s not uncommon nowadays to ask AI to write your grocery list, design your kid’s birthday party invitation, and advise you on how best to taper before your next race, so we’re fairly certain there are a few triathletes out there asking Claude or Chat to draft a strength training program too.

Before you decide to do the same (or perhaps it’s too late and you already have), we thought we’d run an AI experiment where we ask a real human strength coach to assess the bot’s work to help decide how much of the plan is helpful for a multisport athlete, and how much would be a waste of time.

We asked ChatGPT for a strength routine suitable for a triathlete, and about four seconds later it returned a two-day blueprint complete with sets and reps.

Day one covered the lower body and core: squats or goblet squats, Romanian deadlifts, reverse lunges, standing calf raises, dead bugs, and side planks.

Day two went after the upper body and posterior chain: dumbbell bench press or push-ups, rows, lat pulldowns or assisted pull-ups, single-leg Romanian deadlifts, glute bridges or hip thrusts, and Pallof presses. The prescription included three sets of 8-10 reps, for 40 to 50 minutes per session, to be followed for 8-12 weeks.

In a recent development, it all looked perfectly sensible and not too dissimilar to what many triathletes do in most strength workouts. But for a triathlete who’s already squeezing three sports into one week, strength workouts should really be periodized and designed to augment what’s happening in the triathlete’s sport-specific training life (and the off-season is the one time of year when it’s great to do more in the gym, not less).

So with this in mind, we handed the blueprint to strength coach Sam Hengehold, who works with triathletes of all ages and abilities at Kinesis Integrated Performance in Boulder, Colorado. “I’d argue it is not right, but it’s also not wrong,” she states. “The plan is general, but it is not beneficial.”.

Here’s the surprise: Hengehold wouldn’t strike a single exercise from the list.

According to recent reports, “All exercises listed are actually great and could very well be integrated into a triathlete strength routine,” she notes. “The limiter here is the lack of periodization and volume/load variables.”.

Two of ChatGPT’s picks earn special praise:.

Calf raises: “Many triathletes miss this integral exercise in their strength routine,” Hengehold notes. “Lower leg injuries are extremely common with triathletes.” As a general rule, Hengehold wants athletes working toward calf raises at 1.5 times their body weight to build resiliency against injury in the calf, ankle, and foot.

Industry observers note that glute bridges: “A safe way to build power for beginners in strength training,” Hengehold says. They mostly train the glutes and core, the muscle groups that underpin all three disciplines.

So if the exercises are fine, where does the wasted time come in? It’s in how the plan asks you to do them.

Industry observers note that to its credit, ChatGPT suggests lifting less often as race day approaches and adding a little load once the sets feel solid. But the exercises, sets, and reps never change. Your swim, bike, and run training is built in cycles around your races, and Hengehold advises that your lifting should be too.

In the off-season, strength work can take priority and endurance training becomes the base. In race season, that flips: Lifting is there to support your swim, bike, and run, and to keep your body resilient. A blueprint that looks identical in January and July does neither job well.

“Over time, it will just be an energy suck of a session, causing more fatigue in the athlete with minimal benefit,” Hengehold warns.

ChatGPT’s warm-up gets one line: 5-10 minutes of easy cardio, mobility, and lighter practice sets. Hengehold wants something more deliberate, with activation work chosen to prepare you for the main lift of the day.

“Warm-up and activation encourages proper form and oils the muscles,” Hengehold says. “Typically, that would include some sort of dynamic stretching, mobility, or preparation exercise that will aid in the main lift goals of the session. Before squats, for example, that might mean 90/90 hip rotations for hip mobility and banded clamshells to wake up the gluteus medius.” This matters if you want to avoid injury and get the most from every rep.

The substantial, complex lifts belong at the start of the session, when you’re fresh and can control your form. They also work better when paired with an athletic movement, Hengehold says, so the brain learns what the strength is for.

According to recent reports, follow loaded squats with box jumps, for instance, and you reinforce the power you need at toe-off on the run or when pushing watts on the bike. ChatGPT’s plan has no jumps and no explosive work at all.

Recent findings suggest that “Neuromuscular understanding and adaptation is absolutely necessary for triathletes to maximize the benefit of strength training,” Hengehold says. Without it, you get some injury prevention and extra muscle mass, but not much else.

Hengehold named three categories of strength work that matter most for triathletes:.

According to recent reports, core work: Think isometric holds and slow, controlled movements, with deep breathing throughout, to work the transverse abdominal muscles. Hengehold’s picks: planks with alternating shoulder taps, dead bugs, and bird dogs.

In a recent development, unilateral movements: Single-leg Romanian deadlifts, Bulgarian split squats, front-foot elevated reverse lunges, and single-leg calf raises all make each side do its own share of the work. Swimming, biking, and running give a stronger side plenty of chances to cover for a weaker one, and these exercises help break those overcompensation patterns.

Sources indicate that squat variations: Isometric squats (holding the position) and eccentric squats (slowing the lowering phase) are a safe way to build resilience in the lower body and core. The squat is also endlessly adjustable, so it can be tweaked to target whatever you need most.

What you lift, and how, should depend on how far you are from your next race.

Industry observers note that far from race day: This is the time for heavy strength training alongside base swim, bike, and run work. Make complex lifts the centerpiece. Hengehold likes the trap bar deadlift. Get the form and technique down first, then spend a block (typically four to six weeks) building a base with high reps and low weight. Take a deload week, then switch to low reps and heavy weight to build real strength and durability.

In race season: Triathlon training takes over, and strength work drops to maintenance. Unilateral exercises move to the front, scheduled closely around your key sessions and races. Reps and load should go mostly on perceived effort and how you’re feeling, physically and emotionally. Hengehold also stresses mobility work, foam rolling, and stretching during this period.

Recent findings suggest that one last thing no chatbot can do is look at your form. If you’re newly introduced to the weight room, Hengehold recommends having a gym friend or personal trainer check your technique early on: “Bad habits are hard to break and cause damage over time, and the same is true with your swimming, biking, and running.”.

Yet technique is only part of what a generic plan misses.

“Triathletes are some of the most hardworking individuals on the planet and managing training, fatigue, and recovery requires extreme attention to detail,” Hengehold notes. “The time, energy, and hard work need to be maximized to be worth it, which means a generalized strength proposal will not meet the standard. Each athlete is a unique individual with individual needs that require an individualized plan.”.

Sources indicate that none of this is an argument against strength training — far from it. Hengehold calls it “absolutely essential to longevity in sport and health” and recommends it for every athlete. The argument is against spending your limited time and energy on a plan that wasn’t written with you in mind.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The only major program offering free stopovers on one-way partner awards.

It has been revealed that ## Flying Business Class Across Two Continents for the Price of One Imagine settling into a fully flat bed on a Boeing 787-9 somewhere over the Pacific, a warm towel in your hand, Japan behind you and Singapore ahead. You've already spent three days eating ramen in Tokyo — a stopover you added to your award ticket for a mere 5,000 extra points. This isn't a once-in-a-lifetime splurge. This is what the ChooseFI community calls a **nearly free** trip, engineered through one of the most underappreciated sweet spots in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. The Air Canada Aeroplan stopover rule is genuinely one of the last great loopholes in loyalty travel. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop: a business class flight from Toronto to Singapore — routed through Tokyo with a multi-day stopover — retails for **$8,000 to $10,000 in cash**. You can book that same itinerary for **70,000 Aeroplan points** (plus 5,000 for the stopover, so 75,000 total). At a conservative cash value of $8,000, you're extracting **10.7 cents per point** — more than double what most programs offer, and squarely within Aeroplan's documented range of **5.7 to 14.3 cents per point**. To put that in FI terms: if you value your points at even the low end of that range — 5.7 cents per point — 75,000 Aeroplan points are worth **$4,275 in travel**. At the high end, you're looking at **$10,725**. That's a portfolio-level return on the credit card spending and transfer partners you've already been accumulating. What makes this feel different from other premium redemptions is the *shape* of the trip itself. You're not just flying business class — you're building a mini round-the-world itinerary. Tokyo and Singapore in the same award ticket. Two of the world's great cities. Two business class flights. One redemption. The inefficiency here isn't accidental — it's baked into how Aeroplan prices stopovers at a flat 5,000 miles, regardless of where you stop. The program is essentially inviting you to stack experiences on a single award, and the ChooseFI community is the group paying close enough attention to accept that invitation.

The core insight is this: Air Canada Aeroplan uses a fixed partner award chart for Star Alliance flights, and it prices stopovers at a flat 5,000-mile premium regardless of routing complexity. That single policy decision transforms a standard business class award into a multi-destination adventure at a fraction of the combined retail cost.

It has been revealed that here's the mechanism. When Aeroplan relaunched in 2020, it did something most programs had abandoned years earlier: it kept a fixed-rate award chart for partner airlines. While programs like United MileagePlus moved to fully dynamic pricing — where award costs fluctuate with demand — Aeroplan locked in predictable rates for Star Alliance partners. The YYZ to SIN corridor in business class sits at a rate that reflects the geography, not the current demand spike or revenue management algorithm. That's the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community can systematically exploit.

Layer on top of that the stopover rule: Aeroplan allows one free stopover on one-way partner awards for just 5,000 additional miles. A stopover is defined as a connection of more than 24 hours. So your Toronto → Tokyo → Singapore routing becomes a Toronto → Tokyo (stopover 3 days) → Singapore itinerary, all on one award ticket, for 75,000 points total. You've essentially purchased two separate international business class flights for the price of one, plus a nominal surcharge.

According to recent reports, the other critical piece: Aeroplan charges zero fuel surcharges on partner awards. This was a deliberate policy decision in the 2020 relaunch and it's a massive advantage. Programs like British Airways Avios and Singapore KrisFlyer can add $500–$1,500 in surcharges to long-haul business class awards. With Aeroplan, you pay government taxes only — typically $50–$150 on most itineraries.

It has been revealed that you don't need to fly Air Canada or hold an Air Canada credit card to access this. Aeroplan accepts transfers from several major flexible currency programs at a 1:1 ratio:.

Sources indicate that A stopover is a deliberate break in your journey at a connecting city, where you stay for more than 24 hours before continuing to your final destination. Most loyalty programs treat stopovers as separate tickets, requiring you to pay miles for each segment independently. Aeroplan breaks this convention by allowing one free stopover on one-way awards, meaning your connecting city becomes a bonus destination at zero additional mileage cost. For example, a flight from New York to Tokyo with a 5-day stopover in Istanbul costs the same 75,000 Aeroplan points as flying directly — but you get to explore Istanbul for nearly a week as part of the trip. The stopover must be at a connection point that makes geographic sense for your routing, but with 26+ Star Alliance airlines and hundreds of hub cities, the options are vast.

Editor’s Note, November 17, 2026: The Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is currently our “Best Overall” choice. Recently, the Adrenaline GTS 26 dropped, but we’ve not tested it yet. It’s on the list because we loved the 25 so much. The 25 is currently on sale, so grab it while you can.

Some shoes do not have a sexy reputation. Say “stability shoe” to a certain kind of runner and they’ll look like you just suggested they run their next marathon in Crocs. Stability shoes have a reputation problem, and it’s not entirely undeserved. The stability shoes of the early 2000s were clunky, rigid bricks that treated pronation like a disease to be cured with a slab of hard plastic (looking at you, Saucony Grid Azuras). If you ran through that era, I get why you might have a negative, visceral reaction to the type.

Sources indicate that but here’s the thing: Stability shoes got better. Today’s versions are lighter, softer, and not for anything? Cuter. And they are some of the best shoes you can lace up—not just for overpronators, but for anyone whose form gets sloppy when the miles pile up. I’ve known runners who white-knuckle their way through marathon blocks in neutral racers when a little guidance would have saved their knees, their IT bands, and frankly, their sourpusses. Needing support isn’t taking an L. It’s biomechanics.

Sources indicate that at its simplest, a stability shoe is designed to limit excess inward rolling of the foot (overpronation) after your foot strikes the ground. A little pronation is normal and even beneficial; it helps distribute the shock of the impact. But when your ankle collapses too far inward with every step, that torque travels up the chain to your shins, knees, and hips, and over hundreds of miles it can screw up not just your stride, but your long-term health.

Recent findings suggest that neutral shoes let your foot do whatever it wants. Stability shoes help guide your foot into a more correct placement, keeping your body more aligned.

From pounding the pavement to scrutinizing performance in our Shoe Lab, the Runner’s World test editors and wear-testers rigorously tested all of our selections. Our process includes exhaustive market research, analysis of user feedback, and consultations with industry experts. This article was written jointly between our editors Amanda Furrer and Cat Bowen. Bowen tends to pronate, especially when she is tired or in a long training block. She has run in all the shoes on this list with the exception of the Nike Structure Plus.

The Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is one of the most consistent stability shoes on the market, and the silver anniversary enhancement makes a strong case for why this franchise has lasted 25 years. The massive news is in the stack: Brooks added 3 mm to the forefoot and 1 mm to the heel, bringing it to 37 mm and 27 mm respectively, and dropped the heel-to-toe offset from 12 mm down to 10 mm for the first time in the shoe’s history.

The newly introduced heel bevel is the smoothest the Adrenaline has ever had in the opinion of Bowen, who has put serious miles on this shoe. She also feels as though it’s the most balanced this shoe has ever been, and the most balanced on this list.

“Some stability shoes can be so aggressive that the rails can begin to pinch the lateral sides of the foot during long runs,” she notes. “The Adrenaline GTS 25 doesn’t do that, and they still have the cushion and push to power your runs.”.

It has been revealed that DNA Loft v3 foam carries over from the 24, but the extra volume makes the ride noticeably softer underfoot, especially at heel strike. Guide rails are still doing their thing on the medial and lateral edges—reactive, not prescriptive, engaging only when your stride asks for it. The upper is a breathable engineered mesh that has the benefit of preventing overheating and swamp foot with a stretch knit heel collar that locks down without overcrowding.

Though it should be noted that some testers, including Courtney Kazmierczak, feel as though the collar is a hair too high in the back, which requires some trial and error for sock choice.

At 10.6 ounces, it’s not light, but it’s not trying to be. This is a daily trainer for runners who want structure and protection. It’s a shoe that simply does not pinch or bite.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 Review.

Recent findings suggest that this is not a rebuild or huge design change. This is a fine-tuning. The basics are the same; the Adrenaline GTS 26 still uses guide rails as the support system, it has the same stack height, the same drop, the profile hasn’t changed, and the core of the midsole is still the DNA Loft v3 foam.

What did change is that they made it a little bit more breathable by using an engineered mesh upper. The tongue is a bit flatter for a more tuned-in fit, and the heel collar is more refined with a generous pull-tab, which is great for runners with accessibility or limb differences.

Sources indicate that the trade-off here is that it is a teensy bit heavier. We’re talking a few tenths of an ounce difference. And, if I’m being the picky and petty editor that I am? I think the colors and design for this model aren’t as cute. I know, I know, lame thing to bring up, but I really just want a stability shoe in a fun neon. Just because I run like a duck doesn’t mean I don’t deserve fun.

Shop Men’s at brooksrunning.com | Shop Women’s at brooksrunning.com.

According to recent reports, these may be our best value pick, but they’re also some of the most durable daily stability trainers on this list. “I like the durability and stability of these shoes and the fact that they are lighter than previous models,” said shoe tester Lauren Woodall. “I am able to put more miles on these shoes before they need to be replaced than other running shoes.”.

The thing is, even though it’s heavier, and the durability is noticeable, they’re not bricks. They are your easy run shoes, your throw-on-and-go trainers. They’re not the fastest, but they’re not meant to be. When your body is tired, and you need the assistance of that wave plate and the heft of the Enerzy NXT foam, it’s there for you like an old friend holding out a hand. The guardrails on this shoe aren’t superpowered corrections like they were on earlier models, but the gentle effectiveness of them cannot be overstated. Simply put, these shoes just feel really good on your run.

Recent findings suggest that one note about fit: a few of our testers found that you can get a bit of heel slippage in these. However, Mizuno gives you that extra eyelet for a heel lock, and that can absolutely change the fit of the shoe once you lace up. It’s a point worth remembering.

Shop Men’s at usa.mizuno.com | Shop Women’s at usa.mizuno.com.

The Arahi 9 is Hoka-soft, but not max-cush beefy. It’s a versatile model that does double duty as an everyday trainer or tempo shoe. The brand made small tweaks to the upper for a better fit, and made them a little bit less expensive as well. It’s not a huge redesign as much as it’s a refinement.

You forget the Arahi 9 is a stability shoe because of how streamlined the design looks: it’s sleek and a compliment magnet. Hoka modified the upper to dial in the fit a bit more, make it a little more breathable, and adjust some of the hot points felt in the 8.

Invisible to the eye is the H-Frame system that keeps you stable. The H-Frame is a dense piece of foam in the midsole that’s H-shaped. The result is surprising; you’d think the H-Frame would make the Arahi rigid and heavy, but instead the shoe is lightweight and the ride is smooth. Running in it, Furrer felt like she was gliding.

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com.

It has been revealed that there’s something about the Nike Structure Plus that demands attention. In the words of Furrer, “I have a soft spot for this shoe, it’s just so good on long runs.” And that right there is spot on. For the days when you know you have a long run on the calendar, but that long run is full of mixed tempos, hill climbs, potential obstacles, and rough surfaces that you’ll start to feel underfoot after six miles, this is going to be the shoe you reach for. That’s what Nike designed it to handle when it combined the ReactX and ZoomX foams with a dual-zone rubber outsole. It gives you cushion where you need it, flexibility where it matters most, and a nimble feel when you’re dodging pavement cracks.

Arguably the most stylish shoe on this list, Nike really leveled up its stability line with the Structure. It’s also very orthotic-friendly. The collar and the lacing system can handle a lot of pulling, allowing you to get those insoles in correctly. Beyond that, it’s remarkably comfortable as a shoe just to take out and live in. It’s a solid walking shoe, and we love it as a versatile, more cushioned alternative to wear with dressier outfits.

Recent findings suggest that that’s not to say it’s flawless. It’s a bit on the heavier side, and if you’re someone who prefers a shoe that has a lot of responsiveness or bounce, you won’t find it in this shoe. It’s also just a hair on the “runs smaller” side front to back. But other than those small quibbles, it’s a great pair.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

Sources indicate that the differences between the Gel-Kayano 32 and the 33 are key, but not massive. They retooled the design of the support system, employing their FluidSupport tech, which is a bit more malleable than previous iterations, working more with the body’s movements and mechanics. They’ve also softened the foam, updated the fit throughout, and for many runners, it should feel and ride more comfortably.

That being mentioned, it still has all the Asics features you expect and love: a breathable upper, geometry that works to move you forward, and a grippy sole that keeps you upright on wet pavement. It is on the heavier side, but nothing out of the ordinary for a stability shoe, and the collar could have a hair more cushion. However, we love the well-placed heel tab, especially when our hands are sweaty.

The cushion is going to be the biggest win on long-run days. You may not get a ton of energy return, but what you are getting is that added comfort with the guidance that will help you maintain your form and keep you from hating yourself after the run when you’re inevitably lying on the floor propped up on your hands.

Shop Men’s at asics.com |Shop Women’s at asics.com.

The Saucony Guide 19 is a stability shoe that actually earns the word “versatile,” which stability shoes rarely do. Most of them feel like you’re being guided rather than running, but the Guide 19 threads the needle between structured support and genuine responsiveness.

Recent findings suggest that the foundation is Pwrrun foam, which delivers a cushioned but not marshmallow-soft ride. It’s lively enough to handle tempo work without feeling like you’re fighting the shoe, and cushioned enough that you’re not destroyed after 18 miles. The medial TPU guidance frame offers mild overpronation correction without the brick-like rigidity you get from old-school posts. It’s more a gentle steer rather than having the shoe take the reins and navigate your feet for you.

For long runs, the 8 mm drop and 32 mm stack height in the heel keep things comfortable for time-on-feet without creating that spongy instability that kills your form late in a run. For daily training, it’s durable and consistent and a shoe you can lace up without thinking too hard about what’s on your schedule.

And it’s just plain comfortable. At least according to our wear-tester Dave Block, who “can’t remember a shoe that’s felt this great.” And even for tempo days on the track, the fit on this shoe just gets it right. It fits snugly enough that at faster paces it doesn’t feel sloppy.It won’t replace a racing flat, but for runners who want one shoe that handles most of their weekly mileage without drama, the Guide 19 makes a strong case.

Shop Men’s at saucony.com |Shop Women’s at saucony.com.

According to recent reports, what separates the Hoka Rocket X 3 from other super shoes is its broader base and accommodating fit. The shoe has a winged carbon plate to help with propulsion and a dual-density PEBA midsole to provide high energy return and supportive cushioning. An important upgrade: a sticky rubber outsole to prevent slipping and sliding when the race forecast predicts rain or snow.

“These shoes were very stable, which is different for a racing shoe,” indicates tester Shane Houghton, an overpronator. “Most super shoes feel kind wobbly but I felt lower to the ground and never felt in danger of rolling an ankle. When I stand in the shoes I feel flat on my feet and I don’t feel any lateral-rocking. I had no anxiety wearing these during loopy intervals or running around curves. The lacing is tight and like the texture of the ribbed laces. It keeps them from coming undone or loosening while running.”.

Sometimes, shoes that are very much stabilizing or stability-adjacent shirk that term for optics. I can’t prove it, but I believe the Nike ACG Zegamas fit that description.

According to recent reports, I’ve spent months running in these, and as someone who pronates frequently, I can tell you they deliver the structure and support of a true stability shoe wrapped in the rugged outsole of a trail runner. It comes down to that revised last. The Zegama cups the outer rim of your foot so thoroughly that it holds you locked in place, correcting the roll before it starts.

The support straps built into the upper wrap all the way around your foot, the padded tongue and lacing lock your midfoot down, and the heel keeps you planted without any slip. It doesn’t feel neutral, but it doesn’t steer you, either. Instead, it almost feels like it’s anticipatory rather than corrective.

Pair that underfoot security with a grippy Vibram outsole and aggressive lugs that bite into mud and wet rock, and you get the best of both worlds—the stable, planted feel of a stability shoe with the traction to handle whatever the trail throws at you.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

With any piece of running equipment, comfort should be your foremost deciding factor. Here are a few thing to consider before your next shoe fitting:.

1) The shoe should have enough room for your toes to splay in the toebox, about a thumbnail’s width from the front of the shoe to the tip of your longest toe.

According to recent reports, 2) The shoe shouldn’t feel too tight or loose around the midfoot area. There are lacing techniques to help modify your shoe’s width, but you should also consider different widths instead of the standard D (men) or B (women) width.

According to recent reports, 3) A secure heel is also paramount, as slippage can cause blisters. The heel-lock lacing method—threading each lace in the etra eyelet next to it to create a loop, then crisscrossing the opposite laces through the loop to create a “lock”—can give you a more secure fit.

In a recent development, 4) Give the shoes a run at the store or check website’s return/exchange policies. Besides trying on the shoe, the best way to know if it’s comfy is if you run in it, too.

Recent findings suggest that some runners want maximum cushioning underfoot while others want less padding to experience more ground feel. Upcoming foam technology has given us the best of both worlds with plush, high-stacked cushioning that’s lightweight, too. Because of these high stack heights, stability tech is added to help runners run course tangents—and not twist their ankles while doing so.

It has been revealed that still, shoes with thicker cushioning and a high stack (36mm or more) tend to be squishier, making them less stable. Shoes with lower stack heights (32mm or less in the heel) provide a closer-to-the-ground feel and better feedback.

Sources indicate that you don’t have to give up max-cushioning if you’re an overpronator, however. Besides looking for shoes with built-in stability features, like guide rails and stability planes, consider shoes with wide, exaggerated soles, particularly under the heel, and a wider midfoot. Raised sidewalls (the interior padded sides of the shoe) create a snugger fit that will also enhance support, ensuring optimal stability and comfort.

Besides looking for shoes with stability features, you should also consider the type of workouts you’ll be performing in these shoes.

According to recent reports, for speedwork, like tempos and track workouts, lightweight trainers (less than 9 ounces for men or 8 ounces for women) with a curved “rocker” midsole help you surge forward. For everyday runs and longer runs, slightly heavier shoes with more padding provide the comfort and durability that you want on a daily training run. Or if you’re interested in venturing off-road, it’s key to have a trail shoe made for rough, undulating terrain.

Do I actually need a stability shoe?

Stability shoes are specifically designed for overpronation, a type of gait pattern when your foot rolls too far inward upon landing. Flat-foot, low arch runners can also benefit from this extra padding in shoes.

Recent findings suggest that not every flat-foot runner or overpronator may need the extra support, however, especially if their feet only have a slight roll. We strongly advise having your gait evaluated by a professional, such as a podiatrist, physical therapist, or movement specialist. They can confirm if you need motion-specific shoes or an orthotic insert.

The best stability shoes focus on enhancing comfort and promoting a natural gait rather than imposing a harsh, corrective feel. While extra padding may sound like a plus, it can be too prescriptive for some runners. Worst-case scenario: Overcorrecting a neutral stride could increase your chance of injury, rather than make you more comfortable.

If you’re a upcoming runner unsure of your gait pattern, we recommend running in a neutral shoe, like the Hoka Clifton 11s, first.

When should neutral runners consider wearing a stability shoe?

Some shoes with stability tech lend support to late-onset overpronators, i.e., neutral runners whose form becomes erratic midrun due to fatigue. Brands like Brooks and Altra, for instance, use denser foam on the medial and lateral sides of the midsole to help control excessive movement and promote knee and foot alignment, resulting in a more efficient stride.

Is there an adjustment to running in stability shoes?

According to recent reports, as with any running shoe transition, like trying zero-drop trainers for the first time, you’ll want to gradually make the switch if you usually wear neutral shoes. Start with shorter runs and then slowly ramp up mileage or runtime as your body adjusts to the new shoes. Read your body for cues; if you feel some discomfort you may need a slower process before fully committing to stability shoes. Muscle fatigue and pain can also be non-shoe-related and be attributed to overuse. If this is not the problem and it is the shoes, discontinue running in them and talk to a specialist for further evaluation.

Do stability shoes “fix” overpronation?

Recent findings suggest that no. Instead, they support your existing gait pattern. Your shoes can make you feel more comfortable and stable, but it doesn’t change that pattern.

Recent findings suggest that in the words of Test Editor Morgan Petruny: “Keep in mind that a stability shoe is not a cure-all or magic pill. Rather, it is a tool.”.

It has been revealed that overpronation can be due to various factors, including biomechanics, muscle strength, and flexibility, so stability shoes are just one component of a comprehensive approach to managing its negative effects. Strengthening exercises, gait analysis, and proper running form can also play notable roles in that effort.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My longest-lasting pedals are a roughly 10-year-old pair of Shimano SPD XT pedals that have admittedly seen zero maintenance. Those pedals have been effectively abused on everything from getting bashed through rock gardens to long dusty or muddy days on the gravel bike. A few years ago I got my first road bike and switched to a pair of Shimano SPD-SL pedals. Since then I’ve put that bike (and those pedals) through the wringer.

Industry observers note that I tend to stress test gear, even prior to having this job, so I enjoy taking my road bike out on everything from light gravel to singletrack that I have no business on. This means my road pedals have seen similar abuse to my mountain bike and gravel pedals. They’re still in great shape, but they could use a little love. Even pedals only used for road riding will start to get gritty over time.

Then I saw Shimano’s pedal release—not only are the old cleats not compatible with the new pedals, but the price of the new Shimano pedals starts at $200 for the Ultegra model and go up to $300 for the Dura-Ace model.

It has been revealed that after I saw the rollout, it felt like a good time to bring my old generation SPD-SL pedals back to life and while I’m at it, give you a few tips on the process. Here we’ll run through how to service your SPD-SL pedals in under 10 minutes and save you a few hundred dollars in the process.

In a recent development, A quick note on reinstalling the pedals back on the bike: make sure you put the right pedal on the right side and the left pedal on the left side. I know, this sounds obvious. I’ve seen the wrong pedal get forced into the wrong side of the crank too many times, damaging the crank and the pedals to the point that sometimes both need to be replaced. Sometimes pedals are marked with an “L” for left and “R” for right, but you can always double-check to see which way the threads go. Left pedal threads will go up to the left and right pedal threads go up to the right. Then when it is time to reattach the pedals, put some grease on the threads of the crank arm and begin to thread them on by hand instead of starting with the wrench. If you can’t begin to thread the pedal onto the crank threads by hand, double-check the pedal is on the correct side, make sure it’s going into the crank arm straight, and make sure there is no debris in the hole of the crank arm preventing it from threading.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

During a marathon, Juli Windsor admits she doesn’t always get to take in the scenery.

“Most runners can see what's coming ahead, and they can see beyond the shoulders and all the heads,” she said. “For me, my view is hundreds of butts. It’s not the most inspirational view.”.

It’s one difference that Windsor, who is 3-foot-9, has learned to navigate as a runner with dwarfism. But that hasn't stopped her from beating many of those butts in races.

Industry observers note that at the Indianapolis Marathon on November 7, Windsor, 39, ran 3:42:00 to finish in the top third of her 35–39 age group, averaging an 8:28 mile pace. The time was a PR by seven minutes and is provisionally a fresh American record for the T40 para category (a division for athletes with short stature).

In a recent development, windsor was born with an extremely rare form of dwarfism called acromesomelic dysplasia. “Last I heard, I’m one of a million,” noted Windsor, who works as a physician assistant in developmental pediatrics.

Windsor’s run in Indianapolis is more impressive considering that this is part two of her marathoning career. After taking a decade off to raise her two kids in 2014, Windsor has come back even stronger, knocking off more than an hour from her pre-hiatus personal best.

According to recent reports, “I just think the human body is just such an amazing thing,” she said. “And that when asked something difficult of it, what you’re capable of doing can sometimes be really surprising.”.

As a middle schooler, Windsor joined the track team to hang out with her friends and went in with low expectations. But that changed when she beat another runner in an 800-meter race. It was motivating, and Windsor eventually realized that although she couldn’t dust her peers in a sprint, she had exceptional grit and endurance. “I might not be able to outrun them, but I could outlast them,” she remembers.

In her twenties, Windsor set her sights on the marathon—and one marathon in particular. She wanted to become the first person with dwarfism to run the prestigious Boston Marathon. In 2013, her dream almost came true, but as she neared the finish line on Boylston Street, she was forced to stop. Terrorists had detonated bombs at the finish. Windsor was unharmed, but her dream would have to wait.

Industry observers note that the next year, Windsor became the first person with dwarfism to complete the historic race, running 4:43:26. That would be her last marathon for a decade, as Windsor raised two kids and focused on her family.

Recent findings suggest that in 2025, she felt pulled back to the distance. She signed up for the Spinx Marathon in Greenville, South Carolina, where she ran 4:09:51—more than 30 minutes faster than her personal best from Boston.

Not long after, Windsor started working with coach Esther Atkins, a former professional marathoner who coaches with McKirdy Trained. Atkins saw potential in Windsor and had a hunch she could run a lot faster. While unsure at first, Windsor was assuaged when she nabbed another massive personal best, running 3:49:42 at the 2026 Boston Marathon in April.

In a recent development, atkins, who works with about 40 athletes, is impressed by how coachable Windsor is. “She’s always open to trying something different, and very eager to push the boundaries of what she has done before or what she has believed she was capable of,” Atkins remarked.

According to recent reports, “I’m not used to people expecting more of me than I expect of myself; usually it’s the other way around,” Windsor stated. “And that’s how I know I have an exceptional coach. She sees the possibilities and isn’t stumped by my unique challenges.”.

According to recent reports, as a runner with dwarfism, Windsor is presented with obstacles that most runners don’t face. Her cadence, for example, is much higher than the average runner. While 180 steps per minute is a commonly cited target among runners, Windsor averaged 207 steps per minute at Indianapolis, and because her stride length is much shorter, she covers less ground per step. (For reference, Windsor is about the height of an average 6-year-old.).

Windsor also has to navigate crowds carefully—she doesn’t always show up in the peripheral vision of competitors. She generally runs on the right side of the road to improve her visibility and avoid getting tripped up or surprising people as she passes. At larger races, like Boston or Indy, she is able to start a few minutes ahead of the masses to let the race string out.

It has been revealed that and then there are shoes. Windsor wears a kids’ size 13, but it’s hard to find athletic shoes in her size that aren’t Velcro or light-up. She generally sizes up to a size 1 for running shoes and uses custom orthotics. But such small sizes don’t have the bells and whistles of normal running shoes. And super shoes that small don’t exist.

In a recent development, so far, Windsor has liked Asics the best. “I don’t think I fully appreciated the difference of having a good quality shoe until I tried [an Asics shoe] on,” she remarked. “And even just having a gel cushion was like, ‘Is this how everybody else feels? This is what I've been missing out on.’”.

Windsor ran Indianapolis in the GT-2000, although they’re still a little pared down compared to a mass-market adult shoe. “I really wish there were better options and better technology, because I've had to just work with what my options are,” she noted.

Until recently, Windsor wasn’t able to find a GPS watch that fit her wrists. Last summer, she discovered that Garmin made a 42mm watch, which finally allowed her to run without a phone and gave her insights like cadence and stride length. She partially credits the data for her recent improvement.

Recent findings suggest that looking ahead, Windsor has two goals. The first is to qualify for Boston in her age group. Windsor has already nabbed a BQ in the adaptive athlete field, but she’s targeting the able-bodied BQ. She turns 40 next spring, which will bump her to the 40–44 age group. She’ll need to run under 3:35:00—about 7 minutes faster than her personal best—to achieve the standard.

Recent findings suggest that her other goal is to create more opportunities for runners in her Paralympic category. Presently, World ParaAthletics doesn’t sanction running events in the short stature division. USATF recently began to include the marathon in the T40 category, a record which Windsor owns. But the record book isn’t what drives her.

“It's less about competition, more about just setting some sort of a standard, and that records are meant to be broken …” she remarked. “I would love for to open up opportunities for people to at least be curious and give it a try.”.

Industry observers note that next up for Windsor? The Tokyo Marathon on March 7—one week before her 40th birthday.

Kahler has reported on the ground at major events such as the Paris Olympics, U.S. Olympic Trials, Fresh York City Marathon, and Boston Marathon. He’s run 14:20 in the 5K, 1:05:37 in the half marathon, and finished 40th at the 2025 New York City Marathon. He enjoys spotting tracks from the sky on airplanes. (Look for colorful ovals around football fields.).

#125573. After 50 Years of Running, I’m Facing My Toughest Challenge: Having to Let Go of the Runner I Used to Be

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1533 w)
